b64d396d992620af: PETALING JAYA, Sept 9 — Xiaomi has unveiled the Xiaomi 18 Fold in China, taking another shot at the premium foldable smartphone market.
It arrives as a new rival to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, while Apple is widely expected to enter the foldable space with its first foldable iPhone later this week.
As teased in the past week, the Xiaomi 18 Fold gets a compact passport size form factor and it features Leica triple-camera setup.
Xiaomi 18 Fold specs and features

The Xiaomi 18 Fold gets a 5.38-inch outer display with rounded edges which Xiaomi says is designed to be easier to operate with one hand. It uses a 120Hz AMOLED panel that pushes 1712×1168 pixels resolution and it comes protected with Xiaomi’s Longjing Glass 3.0.
When unfolded, you get a 7.58-inch inner display that pushes a resolution of 2364×1672 pixels and 120Hz refresh rate on a flexible AMOLED panel.
Both screens support P3 colour gamut and offer a peak brightness of up to 4,000 nits.
For the folding mechanism, Xiaomi has introduced a new-generation dragon bone hinge using a three-stage connecting structure.

The inner display also uses a dual-layer UTG ultra-thin glass construction. Xiaomi claims the outer 50-micron UTG layer offers 178% higher reliability, while the inner 30-micron UTG layer improves impact resistance by 29%. These are Xiaomi’s own internal claims.
When it comes to dimensions and weigh, it is slightly chunkier than the Galaxy Z Fold 8.
The Xiaomi 18 Fold weighs 219g and measures 5.02mm thick when unfolded and 10.68mm when folded.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
When it comes to dimensions and weigh, it is slightly chunkier than the Galaxy Z Fold 8. — SoyaCincau pic
Under the hood is Xiaomi’s XRING O3 flagship SoC. Xiaomi says the chip features a 10-core CPU, a 16-core GPU and an NPU based on its own large-model architecture.

The Xiaomi 18 Fold is also among the first devices to support LPDDR6 memory but this is only offered for the range topping 1TB model. The lower variants with 256GB to 512GB storage uses LPDDR5X RAM. All Xiaomi 18 Fold are using UFS 4.1 storage.

For photography, there is a proper flagship-class Leica-branded triple-camera setup. It consists of a 200MP Leica main camera with a 1/1.56-inch sensor and f/1.7 aperture and a 50MP f/2.4 ultra-wide-angle camera.

There’s also a 50MP periscope telephoto camera with 3.5x optical zoom and optical image stabilisation, which offers 7x optical-quality zoom. The device can shoot 4K videos up to 60fps and 8K videos at 24fps.
Meanwhile, the front gets a 16MP f/2.2 selfie camera with a 90 degree wide angle.
The Xiaomi 18 Fold is powered by a generous 6,000mAh battery with 20% silicon content. It supports 67W wired charging and 50W wireless charging.
Out of the box, it runs on Xiaomi HyperOS 4.
In China, the Xiaomi 18 Fold is offered in several finishes including red, black and white. There’s also a special ultra-light ceramic version as shown above.
Xiaomi 18 Fold official pricing
The Xiaomi 18 Fold goes on sale in China from 10 September at 10am local time and here’s the official pricing:
12GB + 256GB – Chinese yuan 10,999 (about RM6,628)
12GB + 512GB – Chinese yuan 11,999 (about RM7,230)
16GB + 512GB – Chinese yuan 12,999 (about RM7,833)
16GB + 1TB LPDDR6 – Chinese yuan 14,999 (about RM9,038)
16GB + 1TB LPDDR6 Ceramic Special Edition – Chinese yuan 15,999 (about RM9,640)
So far there’s no word of its international availability. — SoyaCincau
6f7e54eedb5238b2: WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump gave his executive assistant Natalie Harp a US$45,000 cash gift, US media reported Tuesday.
Two other White House employees, Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris, received similar amounts, according to the Washington Post.
The three women described the payments as "Cash Gift for Holidays," the Washington Post reported, citing financial disclosure forms.

Harp has been a near-constant presence at Trump's side in his second term, sometimes typing out social media posts for him and printing out information, a role that has seen her dubbed the "human printer."
She earns US$150,000 a year in her role as the special assistant and executive assistant to the president, according to an annual report to Congress.
A White House spokesperson defended the gifts, citing Trump's "longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides."
They said the gifts were unrelated to any of the individuals' duties, making them "entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards."
48fa658ef8d15af7: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 9 — South Korea’s most expensive film to date, Hope, will hit Malaysian cinemas tomorrow, bringing its ambitious blend of science fiction, action and thriller elements to local audiences.
Reportedly made on a budget approaching 100 billion won (RM302 million), the film is considered the most expensive Korean feature ever produced.
Directed by acclaimed filmmaker Na Hong-jin, Hope follows a village police chief and his rookie deputy as they struggle to protect their community from a mysterious extraterrestrial creature.
Their ordeal begins after wildfires cut off communications, while a local hunting party deep in the mountains finds itself becoming the hunted.
Na is best known for the critically acclaimed 2008 crime thriller The Chaser and 2016 horror film The Wailing, but he has described Hope as a significant departure from his earlier work.
In an interview with the South China Morning Post, Na said he wanted the new film to place greater emphasis on its visual and audio experience.
“Hope is completely different from my previous works,” he said.
“While my past films focused on building up narrative, this time I wanted to make a film that maximises the visuals and audio.”

The film boasts an international cast, including South Korean actors Hwang Jung-min, Zo In-sung and Jung Ho-yeon, alongside Hollywood stars Michael Fassbender, Alicia Vikander, Taylor Russell and Cameron Britton.
On its opening weekend, Hope recorded 1.5 million admissions in South Korea, grossing US$11.3 million (approximately RM46 million) at the box office.
The film is also among the widest releases for a Korean-language film in the United States since Bong Joon-ho’s Oscar-winning Parasite in 2019.
Franchise potential
According to Na, the original screenplay for Hope was considerably longer and was set entirely over the course of a single day.
However, after completing the script, he felt the story was moving too quickly and decided to “essentially chop the script in half”.
The first half eventually became Hope.
That decision could also leave the door open for the story to expand beyond the first film.
Rather than resolving every mystery, Hope establishes its characters, extraterrestrial threat and wider situation while leaving room for a possible continuation.
Final thoughts
Hope held its Malaysia gala screening at GSC Aurum TRX on September 4.

Its production design and the director’s narrative have been among the elements drawing nationwide praise, reflecting Na’s stated intention to make the cinematic experience as visually and aurally immersive as possible.
Hope will be available from tomorrow nationwide in ScreenX, 4DX and IMAX.
f6f5167e8a96ed54: PETALING JAYA: Seorang wakil rakyat DAP menggesa Menteri Besar Negeri Sembilan Ismail Lasim mendedahkan perkara sebenar susulan dakwaan dipaksa menandatangani dokumen bagi menurunkan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar.
Ahli Parlimen Bangi, Syahredzan Johan, berkata dakwaan itu tidak boleh dipandang ringan kerana ia membabitkan kedudukan institusi beraja di negara ini.
“Ismail wajar mendedahkan apa yang sebenarnya berlaku. Pihak berkuasa mesti menyiasat dakwaan ini.
"Isu ini sudah melangkaui Negeri Sembilan. Perkembangan terbaru ini melibatkan soal kelangsungan dan keselamatan institusi-institusi dalam negara serta raja Melayu," katanya di Facebook.
Syahredzan yang juga naib pengerusi kebangsaan DAP turut membangkitkan persoalan mengenai pihak bertanggungjawab melakukan paksaan tersebut, seperti yang pernah dilaporkan media antarabangsa.
“Adakah benar terdapat sosok-sosok dalam Umno yang terlibat dalam episod ini, menurunkan seorang raja Melayu yang mereka sendiri akui sebagai sah?” soalnya.
Terdahulu, Ismail dilaporkan mengesahkan dipaksa menandatangani dokumen proklamasi seperti yang tular di media sosial.
Beliau membuat laporan polis kira-kira 6 petang semalam bagi membolehkan siasatan dijalankan pihak berkuasa.
Semalam, beberapa individu termasuk Undang Luak Johol Muhammed Abdullah dalam sidang media mendakwa Ismail sudah menandatangani dokumen proklamasi untuk menurunkan Tuanku Muhriz.
Mereka mendakwa, Ismail menandatangani dan melengkapkan surat cara proklamasi di bawah Perkara 10(2) Undang-undang Tubuh Kerajaan Negeri Sembilan yang bertarikh 3 Ogos.

Sebelum ini, Sekretariat Undang Yang Empat menuntut pentadbiran negeri, khususnya setiausaha kerajaan negeri, mematuhi proklamasi penurunan takhta Tuanku Muhriz yang didakwa ditandatangani Ismail di Istana Laguna Biru, Port Dickson, bulan lalu.
3363042a55b3ee7e: PETALING JAYA: A DAP leader has urged Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Ismail Lasim to reveal who coerced him into signing a proclamation seeking to remove Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as the state ruler.
DAP vice-chairman Syahredzan Johan said Ismail's claim that he was forced to sign the proclamation was serious and lent credence to a report by Singapore's The Straits Times on the matter.
"Who forced the menteri besar to sign the document? Is it true there were top Umno leaders involved in this episode? That's what Straits Times reported.
"The menteri besar should reveal what actually transpired. The authorities must investigate this allegation.
"This issue has gone beyond Negeri Sembilan now. This new development now involves the continuity and security of the nation's rulers and institutions," he said in a Facebook post.
At a press conference last night, four purported undangs showed a document allegedly containing a proclamation to remove Tuanku Muhriz as Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan.
The document, dated Aug 3, was said to have been signed by Ismail and the four chieftains.
The chieftains, whose positions are also disputed, claimed that Ismail signed the proclamation under Article 10(2) of the Laws of the Constitution of Negeri Sembilan 1959.
Earlier today, Ismail said he signed the document under duress and had lodged a police report yesterday for an investigation to be held.

The menteri besar from Umno rejected the document's validity, saying it did not comply with the processes and procedures provided for under Article 10 of the Laws of the Constitution of Negeri Sembilan 1959.
He previously also denied that Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi was involved in attempts to remove Tuanku Muhriz.
ba2ef9166e574ff5: KUALA LUMPUR: Negri Sembilan Umno has called for a speedy resolution to the issue surrounding the position of Yang di-Pertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir.
Its liaison committee chairman Datuk Seri Jalaluddin Alias said he had no knowledge of rumours that Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim would resign amid the issue.
"As the state Umno chief, I hope this can be resolved as soon as possible.
"I don't know (about the resignation rumours). I'm not in the system anymore. I am no longer a member of the state administration.

"We learnt about what has happened over the past few days through media reports," he told reporters after attending the Umno presidential briefing at the 2026 Umno General Assembly at the World Trade Centre Kuala Lumpur here today.
Asked about Ismail signing the Instrument of Proclamation to remove Tuanku Muhriz, Jalaluddin declined to comment further.
"I have no comment on what the menteri besar has said in his statement. That was his statement," he said.
Earlier today, Ismail claimed he had been forced to sign the document and said he lodged a police report at about 6pm yesterday to allow the authorities to investigate.

He said the state government considered the document invalid, unconstitutional and unenforceable as it did not comply with the processes and procedures under Article 10 of the Negri Sembilan Constitution 1959.
026ee10c1288f555: PUTRAJAYA, Sept 9 — The prosecution has filed an application to stay the Court of Appeal’s decision that granted Datin Seri Rosmah Mansor leave to adduce additional evidence in her appeal against her conviction in the RM1.25 billion solar hybrid project corruption case.
Deputy public prosecutor Mohd Asnawi Abu Hanipah confirmed that the application was filed at the Court of Appeal yesterday.
The application for stay seeks to temporarily suspend the taking of additional evidence pending the disposal of the prosecution’s appeal before the Federal Court.
Mohd Asnawi also confirmed that the prosecution had filed its notice of appeal against the Court of Appeal’s ruling on September 4.
On August 1, a three-member Court of Appeal bench comprising Justices Datuk Azhahari Kamal Ramli, Datuk Dr Choo Kah Sing, and K. Muniandy allowed Rosmah’s application to adduce additional evidence.
The panel ordered that the additional evidence be obtained from prosecution witness Rayyan Radzwill Abdullah through further cross-examination and re-examination.
It also directed that any further evidence introduced by either the defence or prosecution must be confined to matters arising from Rayyan’s additional testimony.
The Court of Appeal further ruled that the additional evidence be taken before a new High Court judge within two weeks of case management, which is scheduled for tomorrow.
Rosmah, the wife of former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak, sought to adduce the additional evidence, consisting of a police report and a statutory declaration affirmed by Rayyan.
In the declaration, Rayyan allegedly claimed that he had been subjected to pressure from the prosecution during the trial.
On September 1, 2022, the High Court convicted Rosmah on three corruption charges under Section 16(a)(A) of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) Act 2009.

She was found guilty of soliciting RM187.5 million and accepting RM6.5 million in bribes from Saidi Abang Samsudin, the former managing director of Jepak Holdings, through her former aide, Datuk Rizal Mansor.
The bribes were an inducement to help Jepak Holdings secure the RM1.25 billion solar hybrid project for 369 rural schools in Sarawak from the Education Ministry.

Rosmah was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment on each charge, to run concurrently, and was also fined RM970 million. She was subsequently granted a stay of execution pending the disposal of her appeal. — Bernama
e85831f5329eeccc: PETALING JAYA: The prices of RON97 petrol, unsubsidised RON95 and diesel will increase by 25 sen from tomorrow, the finance ministry said.
RON97 will retail at RM4.50 per litre, unsubsidised RON95 at RM4.02 per litre, and unsubsidised diesel at RM4.92 per litre.
RON95 under the BUDI95 scheme will continue to be sold at RM1.99 per litre, while diesel will remain at RM2.10 per litre under the BUDI Diesel initiative.

Subsidised petrol under the subsidised petrol control system (SKPS) will remain at RM2.05 per litre, while subsidised diesel under the subsidised diesel control system (SKDS) will retail at RM2.15 per litre.
These prices will be in effect until Sept 16.

The ministry said global crude oil prices rose significantly during the period used to calculate prices under the Automatic Pricing Mechanism amid renewed tensions between the US and Iran, and growing risks of disruptions to petroleum supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.
At the same time, global markets for refined petroleum products remained tight, it said.
It said the government would continue to protect the public and businesses from the impact of global uncertainty, including by maintaining targeted BUDI Madani subsidies for eligible consumers.
From Sept 1, the monthly quota for BUDI95 and BUDI Diesel was increased back to 300 litres from 200 litres.
Eligible owners of diesel-powered pickup trucks and four-wheel-drive vehicles will also receive an additional 100 litres, bringing their monthly entitlement up to 400 litres.
8e418765325f5502: VENICE: A manga film adaptation by acclaimed Japanese director Hirokazu Kore-eda has emerged as one of the frontrunners for prizes at the Venice Film Festival this week.
"Look Back" by the arthouse director, whose past work includes 2018 award-winner "Shoplifters", tells the story of two school friends who dream of becoming manga artists.
The tender coming-of-age tale is based on a popular story by Tatsuki Fujimoto which manga-loving Kore-eda discovered by accident during the Covid-19 pandemic.
"After reading this manga, it was as if someone had pushed me to move forward, had somehow encouraged me," the director told reporters on Monday.

Judged by the reviews of international critics at the festival, "Look Back" has emerged as a favorite alongside "Possible Love" by Korea's Lee Chang-dong and "Wild Horse Nine" by Irish-British director Martin McDonagh.
Film magazine Variety called "Look Back" a "moving tribute to friendship" while the IndieWire website said it drew "rich and dazzling new textures from manga and anime."
Not everyone was convinced, with a review from Screen magazine saying it was "overly sentimental".
In total, 21 productions are vying for the Golden Lion prize for best film at the Venice Film Festival, with others to come before the closing ceremony on Saturday.

Kore-eda is looking to benefit from a global surge in the popularity of manga by choosing the commercially successful work of Fujimoto whose other leading titles include "Chainsaw Man" and "Fire Punch".

"When I was a child, we were told that if all we read was manga, we wouldn’t grow up properly. Now, these days, manga is spreading everywhere ... so we can read it without anyone criticising us," he told a press conference.
The hard-working 64-year-old is a favorite on the European festival circuit.
He presented "Sheep in the Box" at the Cannes Film Festival in May about a grieving Japanese couple who welcome a humanoid robot into their home, but he went home empty-handed on awards night.
"Usually in my head, I'm already preparing for about three movies at a time," he told AFP and other journalists on Tuesday.
He is best-known for his stories about struggling ordinary people, often inspired by real events, including "Like Father, Like Son" or "Nobody Knows".
9d38f7cd47b7411c: KUCHING: The identities of all five victims killed in yesterday's helicopter crash in Long Lellang, Ulu Baram, have been identified through personal belongings found on their bodies.

The victims were Layang-Layang Aerospace pilot Captain Zainol Afiq Bee Sham, 30, from Seremban, Negri Sembilan; Health Ministry doctor Dr Ainul Baraah Kamaruddin, 33, from Kota Baru, Kelantan; nurses Debra Moset, 40, and Jessie Paya Jok, 44; and medical assistant Alexson Adit Henry, 31.

Sarawak Police Commissioner Datuk Mohamud Zainal Abdullah said all five victims were found inside the wreckage of the helicopter, which was registered as 9M-LLF, after it crashed and caught fire at the end of the airstrip.
He said while preliminary identification had been made based on personal belongings, the identities of all five victims were still subject to official confirmation through DNA testing.
"The victims' remains are scheduled to be flown to Miri Hospital for post-mortem examinations and DNA testing," he said.
On the chronology of the incident, Mohamud said authorities received information about the helicopter crash at 3.40pm on Sept 8.
The helicopter had earlier departed Miri at 10.21am before landing in Ba' Lai at 11.39am to carry out an Flying Doctor Service (FDS) mission.
It then departed for Long Siut, Selungo, at 1.41pm and landed nine minutes later to refuel.
The helicopter was believed to have crashed around 3.21pm while attempting to land at the Long Lellang airstrip, coming down at the end of the runway.
The flight to Long Lellang was intended as an overnight stop before the crew continued their next FDS assignment in Tanjong Durian, scheduled for Sept 9.
Following the crash, the Emergency Operations Centre at Miri Airport was immediately activated to coordinate the search and rescue (SAR) operation and confirm the condition of the victims.

The SAR operation and scene investigation involved 67 personnel from various agencies, including the police, Fire and Rescue Department, Health Ministry, Civil Defence Force, Tiger Platoon of the 12th General Operations Force Battalion, People's Volunteer Corps and Malaysia Airports Sdn Bhd.
The scene investigation was also assisted by the Sarawak Criminal Investigation Department forensic team and the Fire and Rescue Department's STORM team from the Miri Zone.
The operation also involved four aircraft and five four-wheel-drive vehicles.

2a238813dc586da4: TAIPEI: Realising that your beloved parent is seriously ill is heartbreaking, but Show Luo always looks on the bright side of life.
In a recent episode of Taiwanese variety show Dee Girl's Talk, the 47-year-old opened up about his mum's battle with Alzheimer's disease which she has been living with for the past few years.
When asked about his 67-year-old mum's condition, the singer became emotional.
"These days, every day is a brand new beginning. In the past, she probably had more worries and stress, such as taking care of stray dogs," he said.
"Now, life is actually a little easier for her. In a way, it's also a wonderful opportunity for her to rest."
There are also days when his mum struggles to recognise him.
"Sometimes she remembers me, and sometimes she doesn't," Luo said.
Naturally, the singer has thought about how heartbroken he would be if his mother completely forgot who he was one day.
Luo recalled that his mum once came to support him at an event, but looked at him and asked: "Where's Show?"
He jokingly replied, "He is at the back," only for his mum to suddenly recognise him and respond: "You're Show! How dare you lie to me!"

The singer said that he is able to face the situation with a relatively relaxed attitude because he understands that, as long as his mother is healthy, it's not important whether or not she remembers him.
"She might forget everything five minutes later, but at least I can keep the memories of all the moments we shared," said Luo.

aa0d4b35dc9da3fb: PETALING JAYA: A consultant forensic psychiatrist told the Kota Kinabalu coroner’s court today he had taken into account the positive aspects of Zara Qairina Mahathir’s diary in his evaluation.

Dr Chua Sze Hung, who was recalled as a witness, said there were several entries about Zara's casual interactions with her friends, and that much of the diary’s contents related to Zara's life at school.

Responding to a question by coroner Amir Shah Amir Hassan, he said his evaluation was intended to identify aspects of Zara’s psychological state that constituted risk factors in relation to her death.

Chua also said numerical scoring was unhelpful in psychological and psychiatric evaluations when asked whether he had conducted a percentage analysis of the positive and negative aspects of Zara’s diary.

“It is not helpful to assign a numerical score when it comes to psychology and psychiatry because we need to understand the nuances and have a descriptive picture of a person’s psychological characteristics and context.

“She had various vulnerabilities, as I had listed in my evaluation. The trauma described and the pain portrayed were significant, particularly when they reached the point where the deceased prayed for her own death and that of others,” he said.
Amir asked if the positive aspects of Zara’s diary were mentioned in Chua’s report.
Amir: You did not include any notes or comments on the positive aspects in your report, correct?
Chua: I did include one or two sections on this, explaining her adjustment to her new environment and its dynamics, but not comprehensively.
Questioned about the possibility of bias in statements given by witnesses, Chua said his evaluation relied on as many sources as possible to assess the validity of the information provided.
He said information obtained from only one source would be identified as such.
He also said he examined the structure of the narratives provided, including their logic, admissions by witnesses that they had forgotten certain matters, and unnecessary explanations.
“It is impossible to eliminate bias completely,” he said.
Zara, 13, died at Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Kota Kinabalu on July 17 last year, a day after she was found unconscious at 4am near a drain at her school hostel in Papar.
The Attorney-General's Chambers ordered her remains to be exhumed for a post-mortem on Aug 8 before announcing a formal inquest into her death on Aug 13.
d3a5d6a6e5e7402b: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 9 — What happens when a music festival packed with thousands of concertgoers becomes the perfect hunting ground for four amateur pickpockets?

That is the playful premise behind Indonesia’s Operasi Pesta Copet, which made its Malaysian cinema debut on September 3 and has been drawing positive reactions from local moviegoers and film reviewers.

Directed by Edy Khemod and distributed in Malaysia by Antenna Entertainments, the film follows four young friends — Ijal (Iqbaal Ramadhan), Adut (Kristo Immanuel), Tia (Zulfa Maharani) and Melodi (Kawai Labiba) — who, each facing their own financial troubles, decide to take the risky route of becoming pickpockets.
Their target? Pestapora, Indonesia’s massive music festival, where they plan to blend into the crowd and walk away with 300 smartphones worth 600 million rupiah.
It is an unusual setting for a heist film, and that seems to be part of its charm.
Since its Malaysian release, local reviewers and moviegoers have described the film as “fresh and fun”, praising its “great cast chemistry” and a festival atmosphere that “feels genuinely alive”.
Another review summed it up neatly as “Pickpockets, but it warms the heart”, while its execution was described as “done very effectively”.
And the festival setting is no movie-set illusion.
Much of Operasi Pesta Copet was filmed during the actual Pestapora festival, putting the cast among tens of thousands of real concertgoers.
The result is a noisy, chaotic, and energetic backdrop that gives the film a sense of authenticity that is difficult to recreate on a soundstage.
The story itself also has an unusual real-life connection.
Khemod, who makes his feature directorial debut with the film, was inspired by an experience from his days as the drummer of Indonesian rock band Seringai.
He encountered professional pickpockets operating at concerts, with some reportedly memorising song lyrics and wearing band merchandise to blend seamlessly into the crowd.
The experience eventually sparked the idea of turning festival pickpocketing into the centrepiece of a comedy.
The film was initially announced as Operasi Pestapora during the 2025 edition of the festival before being renamed Operasi Pesta Copet to make its premise clearer.
Produced by Imajinari, Boss Creator and Angin Segar, the film also goes beyond its comedic premise.
Beneath the jokes and attempted thefts are themes of financial hardship, unemployment, and the difficult choices people make when they feel they have run out of options.
The cast also had to put in some work to make their characters’ criminal skills believable, undergoing about two months of sleight-of-hand training with a professional magician.
Back home in Indonesia, the film opened with 40,706 viewers on its first day.
Some moviegoers speculated that demonstrations in Jakarta and several other areas may have affected attendance, although the film later saw its audience numbers grow.
According to Cinepoint, Operasi Pesta Copet had reached 261,931 viewers as of September 6.

For Malaysian audiences, however, the film appears to be finding its appeal in something simpler: it is a comedy about friendship, desperation and a very unconventional heist — all unfolding in the middle of a real music festival.
And sometimes, a little chaos makes for a pretty good night at the cinema.
Operasi Pesta Copet is still screening in selected Malaysian cinemas.

be21e27c37a96653: Huawei has released the Watch D3, the third generation of its blood-pressure-measuring wearable, as the company continues plowing a relatively lonely furrow in cuff-based technology. The D3 is an intriguing device for anyone seeking more credible blood pressure readings than many smartwatches claim to provide. Where many brands use optical technology to estimate blood pressure, the D series uses a pump built into the watch and an inflatable airbag inside the strap. The D3 is CE-certified as a medical device under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR). This is hardly Huawei's first rodeo: two predecessors have refined the formula and made the device feel less like clinical equipment and more like an ordinary piece of consumer technology. That said, it remains chunky compared with other wearables sold by Huawei and its rivals – the watch body weighs 40 g and is 11.3 mm thick. It's a noticeable improvement over the D2, but still feels like a large device. As it should. It includes a pump, and the removable strap (two sizes come in the box) has a built-in airbag. The Register was given a pair of these watches for a long-term test, and there is a noticeable physical difference between the D2 and D3. Subjectively, it was difficult not to be aware of the D2, but the D3, despite being only a few grams lighter and a few millimeters thinner, is far less obtrusive. Until, of course, it measures your blood pressure, when the tightening strap makes its presence obvious. Although virtually silent, the strap noticeably tightens as the watch measures blood pressure, and the software recommends sitting still, not talking, and placing a hand over your chest while the measurement takes place. The process takes barely a minute and produced plausible, consistent readings during our test. The device supports ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), taking readings at intervals over 24 hours to provide a broader picture of how blood pressure changes during the day and night. A gentle nudge from the watch signals it's time to measure, and away it goes. It also supports blood pressure measurements before and after exercise, and can issue reminders following changes in altitude or temperature. Huawei's Health Community feature allows users to share health information and alerts with family members. Other metrics, such as pulse and blood oxygen, are tracked, but blood pressure measurements are the watch's party trick. Other functionality, such as phone notifications (we paired ours with an iPhone, and calls, messages, and other alerts appeared without drama), is present. However, you will need to install the Huawei Health app to use the device, which might cause some users concern about where their health data is going. We spoke to Rico Zhang, Huawei's president for the product line, via a translator during a launch event in Munich about concerns regarding privacy and data protection. He acknowledged the concern, saying Huawei follows all local policies on personal data and user privacy, and noted that the issue is fundamental "if we want to remain a wearable business in Europe in the future." Zhang gave a similar answer on repairability, saying Huawei followed local regulations. In the EU, battery replacement by consumers is not currently a requirement for wearables sold in the region. Probably also a good idea not to launch a Chinese wearable in Europe with a huge wooden metaphor parked outside. In day-to-day usage, the D3 feels like a slightly larger smartwatch, although we'd contend the user interface is slightly busier than, say, an Apple Watch. The screen is bright (a 1.92-inch display with narrower bezels and 3,000-nit peak brightness), and in our usage we got about five days of battery life. Huawei claims up to six days under typical use, although it says battery life falls to about one day with ABPM enabled. Aside from the user interface, which mainly requires learning new muscle memory, the water resistance is also an issue. Huawei told us the device has an IP68 rating but should not be worn in the shower or submerged for swimming. The company also says it is not water-resistant while taking a blood pressure measurement. Those restrictions are understandable given the inflatable mechanism, but still disappointing. Any water that does get on it also needs to be wiped off to avoid interfering with measurement accuracy. The D3 is a useful device for people who want cuff-based blood pressure readings without carrying a separate upper-arm monitor that sounds like a lawnmower. Its certification as a medical device gives it more credibility than many smartwatch-based alternatives, despite the great strides made with optics over the years, and its styling and size make it feel more like a normal wearable than a health device. The downsides are a busy interface outside the health functions and a design that remains chunkier than other wearables, including Huawei's own, despite efforts to slim it down. The Huawei Watch D3 launches in the UK on September 23 at £399.99. It comes in Black, the version we tested, plus Gold and Mocha Gold. ®
22303ff865f4e2f9: SEPT 9 — Getting a limited reservation can feel like a race. A booking opens, demand rises immediately, and within minutes the available slots may be gone. The frustration becomes greater when the same reservation later appears through an unofficial channel at a much higher price. This is where the term scalper comes into the picture. A scalper is someone who obtains a limited product, ticket or reservation with the intention of selling it again at a higher price.

Scalping is not a new practice, but the digital economy has made it much easier and faster. Reservations can be secured online within seconds and then offered for resale through social media, messaging applications or other online channels. When demand is much higher than the available supply, a limited reservation can quickly become something that is traded for profit.

For consumers, this creates a difficult situation. Someone who was prepared to pay the original price may suddenly have to decide whether to pay more to a third party or give up the opportunity altogether. This raises a more important question about whether consumers are being given a fair chance to access products and services that are already in limited supply.
When scarcity changes consumer behaviour

Scarcity can influence the way consumers think and make decisions. When something is difficult to obtain, people may perceive it as more valuable and feel pressured to act quickly before the opportunity disappears.

This is where fear of missing out, or FOMO, can influence consumer behaviour. A person who would normally refuse to pay a premium may reconsider when the original option is no longer available. The urgency created by scarcity can make consumers focus more on securing the opportunity than on whether the purchase is actually worth the additional cost.
For businesses, this is an important consideration. Creating demand is part of marketing, but the way limited access is managed can also influence how consumers perceive fairness and trust.
The cost goes beyond paying more

The most obvious impact of scalping is the higher price paid by consumers. However, the problem does not end there. Buying from an unofficial seller can also create uncertainty about whether the reservation is genuine, valid or even available.

This can be particularly damaging when consumers become victims of fraud. A transaction that initially appears to offer a solution may instead leave consumers with financial losses and disappointment.

The consequences can also extend beyond an individual transaction. When consumers repeatedly encounter unclear or risky resale practices, their confidence in online transactions may decline. From a consumer welfare perspective, fair access therefore involves more than price. It also involves transparency, security and confidence in the purchasing process.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The author argues that businesses, digital platforms and consumers all have a role in curbing scalping and ensuring fair access to limited reservations. — Unsplash pic
Everyone has a role to play

There is no single solution to the scalping problem. Businesses can begin by reviewing how limited reservations are released and managed. Measures such as identity verification, reasonable booking limits, deposits, waiting lists and clear rules on transferring reservations could reduce opportunities for abuse.

Digital platforms also have an important role. Better reporting mechanisms, warnings about unofficial transactions and systems that can identify unusual booking or resale patterns could help consumers recognise potential risks before making a payment.

Consumers themselves need to be cautious as well. The desire to secure something that is difficult to obtain can sometimes lead people to make decisions they would not normally make. Before paying a third party, consumers should check the seller, verify whether the reservation can legitimately be transferred and consider whether paying a premium is worth the risk.
Where deception or fraud is involved, relevant authorities also need to ensure that consumer protection keeps pace with the way transactions are increasingly taking place online.
Fair access builds consumer trust

The discussion about scalpers points to a wider issue in the digital marketplace. When demand is high and supply is limited, the way access is managed becomes part of the consumer experience. Consumers remember not only what they bought, but also whether the process felt fair.

Businesses therefore need to look beyond the immediate benefits of high demand. A popular product or service can generate excitement, but a reservation system that consumers perceive as easily manipulated may eventually affect trust.

Consumers also have a part to play. Not every scarce opportunity needs to be pursued at any price. Taking a moment to verify a seller, compare options and consider the real value of a purchase can prevent a moment of FOMO from becoming a costly mistake.

Scalping may begin with a limited reservation, but its consequences can extend much further. It can raise questions about fairness, consumer protection and trust in the digital marketplace. Businesses can provide fairer systems, platforms can strengthen safeguards, consumers can make more informed decisions and authorities can ensure that protection remains relevant.
Ultimately, fair access should not be something considered only after consumers encounter a problem. It should be part of the purchasing experience from the very beginning.

* Dr Nurul Fardini Zakaria is a Senior Lecturer in Marketing at the School of Business Management, Universiti Utara Malaysia (UUM), with expertise in consumer behaviour, digital marketing, sustainable consumption and consumer welfare.

8f7a5f1cab1facaf: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 9 — Dengue fever cases nationwide have increased sharply by 66 per cent with 65,979 infections recorded as of Epidemiological Week 35 compared with 39,616 during the same period last year, says Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil.
The unity government spokesman said the issue was among those discussed at the Cabinet meeting today, with the number of deaths due to dengue also showing a significant increase.
He said 62 cases of deaths due to dengue were recorded up to the 35th epidemiological week of this year, compared to 32 cases in the same period last year.
“The Cabinet was briefed on the status of the dengue problem which showed a marked increase compared with the previous year’s.

“The cumulative death toll for 2025 to the 35th week of the epidemic was 32 cases, while for the same period in 2026 there were 62 cases and this is an increase of 93.8 per cent,” he said at a press briefing that was broadcasted live after the Cabinet meeting in Putrajaya today.
Fahmi, who is also the communications minister, said the Cabinet also discussed measures to address the hike in cases, including the implementation of gotong-royong programmes soon.
He said the Housing and Local Government Ministry (KPKT) will be in charge of organising the programme, especially in areas identified as red zones or where an outbreak is occurring.
“The KPKT will start the gotong-royong programme in the next few months, and this will be followed up with a statement from the ministry,” he said.
Meanwhile, Fahmi said the Cabinet was also briefed on the success of the Wolbachia mosquito breeding programme in Putrajaya.
However, he said the Cabinet was also informed about the effects of “fogging” activities on Wolbachia mosquitoes, which are used as a method of dengue control.
“The Wolbachia mosquitoes, which are capable of inhibiting the reproduction and spread of the Aedes mosquito dengue virus, can die during the 'fogging' process.
“With that, efforts to promote gotong-royong programmes need to be given attention, especially in locations identified as high risk,” he said.

The Wolbachia mosquitoes are regular Aedes aegypti mosquitoes that carry a natural, safe bacteria called Wolbachia, which blocks them from spreading dangerous viruses like dengue, Zika, and chikungunya.
d33f56bdf8060e56: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 9 — Umno today accused Pakatan Harapan (PH) of applying a double standard on royal pardons after the coalition said those convicted in high-profile corruption cases should serve their full sentences.

086e1bee58d139c9: SAN FRANCISCO, Sept 9 — Apple is expected to unveil a slew of new and updated devices, including a long-rumoured foldable iPhone, when it holds its annual late-summer hardware event today in Cupertino, California.
It will also be the first major event under new chief executive John Ternus, who took over from outgoing CEO Tim Cook on September 1.

Ternus, 51, joined Apple’s design team in 2001 and worked his way up to leading the engineering teams behind Apple’s entire product lineup, including the iPhones that generate most of the company’s revenue.
The event, which Ternus promised would be “phenomenal” in his first company-wide email as CEO last week, will kick off at 10am local time (1700 GMT/1am Malaysian time).
The tech giant is expected to finally reveal a long-awaited foldable iPhone, currently rumoured to be called the iPhone Ultra, which will start at US$2,000 (RM8,118), according to reports.
Like Samsung’s foldable smartphones, Apple’s device will have a smaller external display when closed and a much larger screen that unfolds when the phone is opened.
The format essentially combines the portability of a smartphone with the larger display of a tablet, offering users a larger screen without carrying a tablet-sized device.
The foldable will be a test for Apple, which has not launched a breakout hit since the AirPods 10 years ago.

Samsung launched the industry’s first mainstream foldable smartphone, the Galaxy Fold, in 2019. The South Korean company released an updated model, the Galaxy Z Fold, last year at a starting price of US$2,000.

Foldable smartphones make up a tiny fraction of the market, at less than 2 per cent of global shipments, but Apple could take 31 per cent of that demand by the end of the year and reach 40 per cent by 2027, according to research firm IDC.
“Apple’s foldable iPhone is very likely to shift the competitive dynamics both in China and global markets,” IDC research associate Kiranjeet Kaur told AFP.
The foldable iPhone’s release comes as demand for powerful chips amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom has created a supply chain crunch, pushing prices higher across industries.
As a result, smartphone shipments will decline by more than 16 per cent this year while the average cost jumps more than 27 per cent, according to IDC.
“Foldable phones are not immune to the memory supply shortages, but the relative impact is lower considering these phones are already priced in the higher-range,” Kaur said.
In what would be a first for Apple, it is unclear whether the company will launch a new entry-level iPhone this year.

According to various reports, the company might only unveil two higher-end versions of its next series: the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. A more affordable base version, the iPhone 18, might not launch until next year.
The foldable Ultra will be around the size of a passport when closed and have only two camera lenses, a regular and an ultra-wide lens, according to Bloomberg.
An improved version of Siri, powered by AI, will be integrated into many of the new devices announced, which could include watches, AirPods, an Apple TV box and the HomePod mini.

The company might also launch a 7-inch device with a screen meant to act as a smart home hub, Bloomberg reported, though it is unclear whether that will be unveiled Wednesday or later this year. — AFP

3d4a1143bfe0493b: SEPTEMBER 9 — The final quarter of 2026 is shaping up to be considerably more difficult than many governments had hoped.

Brent crude has broken above US$100 a barrel. The conflict between the United States and Iran remains unresolved. The Strait of Hormuz continues to be the critical pressure point in the global energy system.
Meanwhile, across several Western democracies, the politics of national identity, immigration and economic grievance are strengthening parties and movements of the far right.
These may appear to be three separate developments. They are not.

For Asean, they represent three interconnected pressures: the return of inflationary anxiety, the persistence of geopolitical instability in West Asia and the expansion of increasingly polarised identity politics across the international system.
Asean will have to navigate all three simultaneously.
The most immediate challenge is inflation.
When Brent crosses US$100 a barrel, the consequences do not remain confined to petrol stations. Energy is embedded throughout modern economies.
Higher crude prices increase transportation and logistics costs. Aviation becomes more expensive. Electricity generation can face additional pressure in economies dependent on imported fuels.
Fertiliser, petrochemicals, plastics and manufacturing costs can rise. Eventually, some portion of these increases works its way through supply chains into consumer prices.
The danger therefore lies not simply in expensive oil.

It lies in the possibility that another energy shock will arrive precisely when the global economy has yet to develop complete immunity against the inflationary disruptions of the first half of this decade.
This presents central banks with an uncomfortable dilemma.
If inflation accelerates again, monetary authorities may have less room to reduce interest rates. In the United States, renewed inflation could even intensify arguments for tighter monetary policy.
Higher American rates would reverberate far beyond the United States through currencies, capital movements, borrowing costs and financial markets.
Asean cannot insulate itself completely from such developments.
Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam, Singapore and Malaysia participate deeply in international trade and finance.
A stronger dollar combined with expensive energy can place pressure on currencies and increase the domestic cost of imports.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

For Asean, they represent three interconnected pressures: the return of inflationary anxiety, the persistence of geopolitical instability in West Asia and the expansion of increasingly polarised identity politics across the international system. — Picture by Firdaus Latif.
Malaysia possesses some protection through its energy resources and existing mechanisms for managing domestic fuel costs.
But even Malaysia cannot escape the secondary consequences of prolonged international energy turbulence.
The second anxiety is geopolitical.
The continuing confrontation involving Iran has become more than another episode of Middle Eastern instability. Its importance derives from geography.
The Strait of Hormuz remains one of the world’s most consequential maritime arteries.
A substantial share of internationally traded petroleum and liquefied natural gas must pass through this narrow passage.
Iran therefore possesses leverage even when it cannot achieve outright military superiority against the United States.
Washington, conversely, possesses enormous financial, military and technological capabilities to place pressure on Tehran.
The result is an imbrogliotic situation in which neither side can easily impose its preferred outcome without accepting potentially enormous costs.
Iran needs energy revenues.
The United States wants to constrain Tehran’s ability to convert those revenues into strategic power.
Yet the more unstable the Strait of Hormuz becomes, the greater the damage inflicted upon countries that have nothing whatsoever to do with the original confrontation.
Asean belongs squarely in this category.
The region depends upon open sea lanes stretching from the Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean through the Strait of Malacca into the South China Sea and wider Pacific.
Energy security in West Asia is therefore inseparable from economic security in Southeast Asia.
Asean should consequently continue supporting diplomatic efforts aimed at restoring the normal movement of commercial shipping through Hormuz. This is not taking Iran’s side or America’s side.
It is defending the fundamental Asean interest in keeping the arteries of international commerce open.
But there is a third pressure that may prove more politically complicated.
Economic insecurity has historically created fertile conditions for identity politics.
When households feel squeezed by food, housing, transportation and energy costs, political arguments frequently become less technocratic and more emotional.
Questions about wages can become arguments about immigration. Debates about industrial competitiveness can become accusations against foreigners.
Economic uncertainty can strengthen political movements promising protection through nationalism, borders and increasingly restrictive definitions of national identity.
The strengthening of far-right politics in parts of Europe should therefore be watched carefully from Southeast Asia.
Asean should not assume that these political currents are geographically confined.
Identity politics travels.
Social media accelerates it. Artificial intelligence can magnify it.
Disinformation can weaponise it. Economic hardship provides fertile terrain in which it can grow.
Southeast Asia itself contains extraordinary ethnic, religious, linguistic and political diversity.
The region’s stability has depended partly upon the ability of governments and societies to prevent those differences from becoming permanently zero-sum.
That achievement cannot be taken for granted.
A prolonged period of high living costs combined with slower global growth would inevitably place greater pressure on governments.
Under such circumstances, political entrepreneurs may discover that mobilising identity is easier than explaining complicated international economic conditions.
This is precisely what Asean must resist.
The difficult final quarter of 2026 therefore requires more than conventional economic management.
Asean needs strategic sobriety.
Governments must contain inflation without unnecessarily suppressing growth.

They must protect vulnerable households without allowing fiscal commitments to become permanently unsustainable. They must diversify energy sources and accelerate regional energy cooperation, including the Asean Power Grid.
At the same time, Asean diplomacy must continue supporting de-escalation in West Asia and the restoration of predictable commercial navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
Most importantly, Asean governments must avoid allowing external economic shocks to become internal political fractures.
The three pressures are connected.

War creates uncertainty. Uncertainty raises energy costs. Higher energy costs feed inflation. Inflation weakens household confidence. Economic frustration can then be redirected towards ethnic, religious, migrant or ideological targets.
That is how an external geopolitical crisis can eventually become a domestic political problem thousands of kilometres away.
Asean has survived many crises because it understands that stability is not created by eliminating every disagreement. It is created by preventing disagreements from cascading into something larger.
The end of 2026 may test that instinct again.
The danger is not merely that Brent has crossed US$100.
It is that expensive energy, an unresolved Iranian imbroglio and increasingly strident identity politics are beginning to reinforce one another.
Asean cannot determine what Washington and Tehran ultimately decide. Nor can it determine the political direction of Europe or the United States.
But Asean can determine how resilient Southeast Asia will be when these external pressures arrive.

The final quarter of 2026 is looming as a difficult one. Asean should prepare accordingly—not with alarm, but with economic discipline, diplomatic persistence and an unambiguous refusal to allow identity politics to turn international turbulence into regional division.
*Phar Kim Beng, PhD is the Professor of Asean Studies at International Islamic University of Malaysia and Director of Institute of International and Asean Studies (IINTAS).

e4c4d511a5f3d505: Switzerland's Federal Chancellery is preparing to offer a FOSS workplace suite to some 3,000 employees – but the Swiss Armed Forces are pushing ahead faster still. European interest in digital sovereignty isn't limited to the European Union: the Swiss Federal Chancellery plans to offer selected government employees a FOSS alternative that will run alongside Microsoft 365. The chancellery is launching the program with an initial 3,000 staff, out of some 47,000 federal employees. The platform is expected to become available to about 3,000 selected employees from the end of 2027, with the first phase forecast to cost CHF 9 million (£8.2 million, $11.1 million). For comparison, Swiss Radio reported last year that the federal government had spent CHF 1.1 billion (£1 billion, $1.4 billion) on Microsoft licenses. The program follows the BOSS Proof of Concept feasibility study, which began last year and tested browser-based FOSS tools with 172 users. The English version of the report says: "Functions examined included document editing, email, calendar, contacts, tasks, file storage, audio and video conferencing, chat, and identity and access management." The study carefully spells out four limits to its scope: It would not replace Microsoft 365 It would not have 1:1 functionality It would not have full M365 compatibility It would not be permanent infrastructure It's important to make this stuff plain right at the start. Back in 2022, in a piece whose working title was You can't buy software, this vulture mentioned a member of one of his online communities who wanted to replace Microsoft software with free software – but demanded complete fidelity, including intact imports of all his Outlook files. This kind of exact and perfect match is basically impossible, and the four bullet points above strike us as a good effort at managing users' expectations. The Chancellery concluded that the browser-based suite was suitable in principle for key standard tasks, although it also identified technical and operational limitations. The next phase will cover less than 10 percent of federal employees and is expected to take about 15 months. The plan is to use the openDesk suite from the German state-owned enterprise ZenDIS. This is the same collaboration suite that we reported Mecklenburg-Vorpommern was adopting in July, following neighboring Schleswig-Holstein in 2025. The move is part of the Swiss government's Digital Switzerland Strategy 2026, announced in Bern at the end of 2025 – less than a month after its Federal Council's report on Swiss digital sovereignty. They also follow the 2024 introduction of the Federal Law on the Use of Electronic Means for the Fulfilment of Governmental Tasks – or EMBAG for short. The government has a fresh interest in open source – indeed, the Chancellery maintains an online catalog of its own open source tools. Back in July, Heise reported in English that the Swiss Armed Forces were making similar moves. It cites a German-language report from Swiss publication Republik, Die Cyber-Spezialisten des Bundes kehren Microsoft den Rücken – The federal government's cyber specialists are turning their backs on Microsoft – which has more details. The military is moving faster: Republik says it aims to complete the migration by October 2026 – next month at the time of writing. Again, there is a local precedent – this time, from Austria. In September last year, representatives of the Austrian military presented a talk at the LibreOffice Conference in Budapest: Migration to LibreOffice in the Austrian Armed Forces (ÖBH). Last month, the ÖBH gave a long interview to the Document Foundation about how and why: part 1 and part 2. ®

40f21c1be0c5114d: Battery installations hit a new record in the US in the second quarter of 2026. In total, 20.2 gigawatt-hours of new capacity came online, according to a new report. That’s enough to supply the daily electricity needs of about 700,000 homes.

The surge is putting the country on a trajectory to see 71 gigawatt-hours of batteries installed in 2026, a 20% increase over last year. This growth is being driven by a combination of cheaper batteries and an urgent need for more energy storage capacity as renewables such as solar and onshore wind power are added to the grid.

Massive, utility-scale systems are leading the way; they’re responsible for most of the record-setting quarter. Seven new gigascale battery installations (those with a capacity of over one gigawatt-hour) came online during the three-month stretch, according to the report, published by Benchmark Mineral Intelligence and the Solar Energy Industries Association.
“It really came down to a handful of big projects,” says Shan Tomouk, energy storage and energy lead for Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

But there was also growth in the category of so-called behind-the-meter batteries, which include both residential and industrial battery storage systems. These projects, generally smaller than utility-scale installations, are typically owned and operated by homeowners or businesses rather than utilities or power providers.

In the behind-the-meter category, data centers led the way, making up about three-quarters of new batteries in the commercial sector. But residential batteries saw a sharp slowdown. These systems are often installed in homes to store power from solar panels or serve as a backup source in case of a blackout. Home installations are projected to drop by 16% in 2026 compared with last year, according to the report.

That drop happened largely because a tax credit that helped subsidize home battery systems ended in 2025, Tomouk says. Home installations should recover by the end of the decade, he adds. And tax credits for nonresidential batteries have largely survived.
Overall, batteries are a bright spot in energy right now. “This is one of the strong sectors in the US,” says Isshu Kikuma, an energy storage analyst at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

As the battery market continues to grow, one major trend to keep an eye on is a move toward US-made technology. Today, nearly all the systems coming online use cells made in China, though some are put together into complete energy storage systems in the US.

Tariffs were already pushing the US energy storage industry toward domestic production. And beginning this year, energy storage tax credits required projects to limit their reliance on batteries imported from China. There’s a lot of manufacturing capacity set to come online in the US, though these factories probably won’t be able to meet demand until at least 2030 or so, Tomouk says, so prices could tick up.

2f842d11c33cd455: Plug a phone into a modern charger and the first 10 minutes are impressive. The next 20 are not.

This is not a defect. It’s the connected device protecting itself. As temperature rises during charging, a smartphone’s battery management system reduces the current it will accept, because heat accelerates the chemical degradation that permanently reduces battery capacity. The charger may be capable of delivering more, but the device simply stops taking it.

For anyone building products in the portable power category, this creates an uncomfortable gap between specification and experience. A device rated at 25 watts is accurate in the sense that it can deliver 25 watts. Whether it delivers 25 watts for the duration of a charge is a different question, and one the specification does not answer.
The specification gap
The gap matters commercially because it is invisible at the point of purchase and obvious in use.

Consumers compare wattage figures on packaging. They don’t compare thermal curves, because thermal curves are not published publicly. The result is a category where products differentiate on a number that describes peak output rather than sustained output, and where the actual user experience of two products with identical specifications can diverge substantially.

This is particularly acute in magnetic wireless charging. Inductive power transfer generates heat at both the transmitting and receiving coils, and the magnetic attachment that makes these products convenient also places the heat source in direct contact with the device it is charging. Convenience and thermal performance are working against each other by design.

The industry’s response for the past several years has been materials science. Graphite sheets, thermal interface materials, conductive housings, and heat-spreading layers have all improved how efficiently accumulated heat moves away from the source. Each generation has been incrementally better than the last.

But passive dissipation has a structural limitation: it can only move heat that has already been generated, and only as fast as the surrounding air will accept it. In a sealed, pocket-sized enclosure, that ceiling arrives quickly. Improving the materials slows the rate of temperature rise. It does not prevent the temperature rise.
Moving from dissipation to removal

The alternative is active thermal management, which is standard in stationary electronics and largely absent from portable ones for reasons that are easy to understand. Fans add volume, weight, moving parts, and noise. In a product category defined by portability, each of those is a meaningful cost.

At Anker, which manufactures charging and power products, engineering teams spent the past several development cycles working on whether that tradeoff could be made acceptable rather than eliminated. The approach involves several interacting systems: a micro centrifugal fan, dual airflow channels routed to avoid interference with the magnetic array, a three-layer graphene heat-spreading layer, and a control algorithm that modulates fan speed based on real-time temperature and battery state rather than running at a fixed rate. The result is that the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro has become the world’s fastest and coolest wireless power bank.

In internal testing, at 77 °F (25 °C) ambient, the back of the power bank stays below 96.8 °F (36 °C) throughout wireless charging, 21.6 °F (12 °C) below the international standard limit of 118.4 °F (48 °C), for a comfortable grip. Comparable magnetic power banks in the same testing typically reached 113 °F (45 °C) or higher within 20 minutes. The functional consequence is that the connected device does not reach the threshold at which it begins reducing charge acceptance, so 25 watts of Qi2.2 magnetic wireless charging is delivered as a working rate rather than an opening rate. In practice, an iPhone 17 Pro reaches 50% charge in 25 minutes. The Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro’s premium performance in both charging speed and thermal management is certified by SGS, an independent testing and certification company.

The same principle applies in reverse. Recharging a power bank generates heat too, which is why devices in this category are often slow to recharge, leaving users with an empty accessory at the moment they need it. Active cooling during input allows the unit to accept 45 watts and reach 80% in 52 minutes.
What this suggests about the category
There is a broader pattern here worth naming, because it is not unique to charging.

When a category improves along a single axis for long enough, the constraint usually migrates somewhere else. Charging spent a decade optimizing power delivery. Power delivery is now, for most practical purposes, solved: the electronics can supply more energy than the receiving device is willing to accept. The binding constraint moved to thermal management, and the industry continued optimizing the axis it had always optimized, because that is the axis the specifications describe.

Recognizing when a constraint has moved is difficult precisely because the old metric keeps improving. Wattage figures have continued to climb. Products have continued to get faster on paper. The measurement stayed valid while quietly ceasing to describe the thing users experience.

For product organizations, the practical question is whether their specifications still measure the constraint or merely measure the capability. The two align until the constraint shifts and specifications rarely shift with it.
The transparency problem

A second implication follows from the first. If sustained performance differs meaningfully from peak performance, and if only peak performance is disclosed, then buyers cannot evaluate the products in front of them.

This is one reason Anker is adding displays on charging products. The Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro shows real-time power, temperature, battery level, and estimated time remaining. Some of that is user convenience. But some of it is a Anker stating a deliberate position—this category deserves to have the complete and accurate data made transparent to all.

Anker expects independent reviewers to test these claims and considers our internal numbers to be the correct outcome. The gap between specification and experience closes faster when the experience is measurable. The Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro will be available in the U.S. on September 17, 2026.

b39b39b293cde37a: From Azam Mohd
Umno’s 2026 general assembly should be judged less by which coalition it prefers than by whether the party can prove that participation in government has made it more useful to voters.
The real test is converting access to power into public confidence before the 16th general election.

The assembly, running from Sept 9 to 12, brings together more than 6,400 delegates. Umno secretary-general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki has said 157 motions from divisions include the party’s political direction and cooperation within the unity government.
Delegates are, therefore, examining whether Umno’s present arrangement strengthens its claim to represent Malay interests while governing a plural country.

That distinction matters. Since GE15 produced a hung Parliament, Umno has operated within a coalition it once opposed electorally. The arrangement helped provide federal stability, but stability alone cannot rebuild political loyalty. Malay voters who moved elsewhere did not necessarily abandon Umno because of one coalition formula. Their decisions also reflected leadership credibility, governance, economic pressure and responsiveness to everyday concerns.
This makes the debate over staying in or leaving the unity government incomplete. Coalition arithmetic is important, but changing partners cannot substitute for rebuilding trust.

Barisan Nasional secretary-general Zambry Abdul Kadir has reaffirmed the coalition’s commitment to maintaining the government until an election is called, even as Umno leaders discuss the merits of an earlier GE16. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said an earlier election can be considered while stressing economic recovery, public welfare and combating corruption.

Umno, therefore, faces two responsibilities simultaneously. It must preserve enough political independence to remain recognisable to its traditional base while demonstrating that its role in government contributes to national stability and effective administration. If it appears merely attached to federal power, it risks losing identity. If it pursues confrontation simply to display independence, it risks weakening the stability it helped create.
The stronger route is performance politics.

For voters, coalition arguments eventually collide with household economics. Wages, food costs, housing, employment opportunities, education and social mobility shape political confidence more directly than elite negotiations.

The pre-assembly Malay Education Convention, where Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi outlined goals linking Bumiputera education more closely with recognised industrial competencies and workplace learning, points toward a more durable political language: measurable advancement rather than symbolic reassurance.

But announcements require accountability. Umno should use its position in government to demonstrate outcomes that can be independently assessed: skills pathways, employment prospects, assistance for vulnerable households, transparent administration and opportunities for younger Malays without framing national prosperity as a zero-sum ethnic contest. Malay advancement and an inclusive Malaysian economy need not be competing objectives.

The assembly also presents a leadership test. Zahid described the 2026 general assembly as a forum for delegates to bring the voices and responsibilities of the grassroots. That principle carries consequences. If grassroots concerns are genuinely central, uncomfortable views about alliances, leadership, candidate quality and government performance must be heard rather than converted into ceremonial consensus.

GE16 preparation should consequently begin with candidate credibility and constituency intelligence, not slogans. Umno’s machinery remains an organisational advantage, but machinery cannot manufacture trust indefinitely. Candidates must possess local legitimacy, clean reputations, policy competence and the ability to communicate across generations. Younger voters inhabit a political environment where information travels instantly and institutional loyalty cannot be assumed.

Umno should also confront an evidence gap. Public claims about a return of Malay confidence require constituency-level proof. Electoral gains, membership enthusiasm and crowded political gatherings measure different things.
The party needs analysis of voter transferability, turnout, age cohorts, marginal constituencies and reasons voters change allegiance. Without such evidence, optimism can become strategy by anecdote.

This year's Umno general assembly, therefore, matters not because it can settle Umno’s future in four days, but because it can clarify the standard by which that future should be measured. The question is not whom Umno stands beside, but what it delivers.

Beyond the assembly, its renewal will depend on turning relevance into governing usefulness. If Umno can connect Malay confidence with competent administration, economic opportunity, institutional integrity and national stability, it can approach GE16 with a defensible proposition.
If coalition positioning remains the main story, the party may leave Kuala Lumpur more united internally without becoming more persuasive electorally.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

5681caf98ef3f355: One of the few proven use cases for generative AI is automating customer service inquiries to reduce costs even further than it’s been possible to achieve by offshoring jobs to low-wage companies like the Philippines – which yesterday bet that its outsourcing industry will thrive even as it plans a massive investment in AI. The nation’s government yesterday delivered the PAIIM – aka the Philippines AI+ Infrastructure Masterplan [PDF], a policy that calls for $34.4 billion of investment in infrastructure, connectivity, and datacenters. Current government programs and private investments dedicated to funding network and energy spending already cover $18.2 billion of the planned spend. The government hopes the remainder “will be mobilized through targeted public investment and private sector participation, particularly for hyperscale AI datacenter infrastructure.” The plan assumes private enterprise will invest $21 billion of the total spend. The likes of Amazon, Google and Microsoft currently spend roughly $20 billion on AI infrastructure each quarter. Chinese clouds also expect to spend tens of billions each year. The Philippines is bidding for less than a month of their combined spending to fuel its national plan. The Philippines’ government nonetheless thinks this plan will turn the nation into a regional AI hub and see the national datacenter fleet surge from today’s 50MW to 1.5 GW by 2033, and for the new bit barns to house around 152,000 GPUs. Again, these are small numbers: American and Chinese AI players have committed to acquire and operate millions of GPUs that require multiple gigawatts of energy. Government officials said the plan means the Philippines can compete with regional competitors Singapore and Thailand. They didn’t mention nearby Malaysia, where the Johor datacenter province already has almost 4GW of datacenter projects in place, with similar capacity in the planning and construction pipeline. Citizens have been told that the plan will see over 1.3 million professionals receive training on how to use AI, and will generate half a million AI-related jobs – 175,000 of them working on AI infrastructure projects. “These investments will further produce spillover benefits such as improved public service delivery, greater international connectivity for all businesses, and enhanced cybersecurity and data governance frameworks in line with global best practices,” the plan promises. Those outcomes are made possible, the plan suggests, by the fact that the nation already has a million-strong tech workforce – including its outsourcing industry that will apparently both make the AI plan possible and benefit from it. “PAIIM does not position AI as a replacement for the Philippine IT-BPM industry;” the policy document states. “Rather, it enables the sector to move up the value chain by using AI for first-level, repetitive, and data-intensive interactions while empowering Filipino workers to handle complex, empathy-driven, and higher-value customer experience functions.” That’s a very old assumption about the impact of automation on customer service. Yet the Philippines owes the existence of its business process outsourcing industry to the fact that automation alone didn’t drive down the cost of customer service to levels that some businesses were willing to pay. And AI will likely enable even more automation at even lower costs. ®
