0003a86f9740b0fb: Malaysians recently enjoyed a public holiday on our National Day. Many also enjoyed the week-long school holidays while some got a hattrick of celebrations – an extra day for Selangor residents for the state topping the medals table at the recent Sukma inter-state games.
It’s a pretty good deal for many, including state politicians who got to give out the good news to Selangor’s residents at no cost to themselves because it’s the employers who foot the bill.

As a retiree I didn’t get to enjoy an extra day's holiday nor did I get holiday pay for working on the day. But at least I’m not an employer who has to foot the extra costs or deal with the disruptions caused by it.

Declaring a casual public holiday is a misguided attempt to buy goodwill from the rakyat. Either elections must be around the corner, or it’s become a reflex action for an ad hoc public holiday to be created.

The economy doesn’t benefit from this: costs go up and benefits are reduced to society at large. But you cannot argue about giving workers additional respite from their days at the office or factories. We have laws that require us to observe public holidays, of which we have a lot, scheduled and ad hoc, plus personal paid vacations, with most companies providing more than what is stipulated.

I guess if somebody very important passes away, or we achieve something truly epic – we win the World Cup! – then perhaps a public holiday is deserving. But lets examine the reason public holidays are declared in the first place.

They are meant to allow us to observe such holidays appropriately – perhaps by celebrating, marching in the street, holding celebrations, visiting families and friends or fulfilling cultural or religious obligations.

If you stay at home and don’t celebrate the event, then why are you deserving of a paid day off? I can tell you if Malaysia wins the World Cup I’ll be running myself ragged for perhaps days in an orgy of celebrations, and I certainly would welcome the public holiday.

But I remember a state declared an ad hoc holiday in three consecutive years purely because it made it to the final of the Malaysia Cup football competition. Not won it, just made it to the final, which it managed to lose each time.

I remember the business disruptions, and especially the withering looks from my foreign bosses and colleagues signalling – what kind of rubbish is this? I had no good answer then, and certainly none now either.

Disruptions didn’t just happen to businesses; they happen to normal people too. Most government and business services are closed with hardly any notice. Think about the disruptions to our everyday life in our dealings with the courts or passport offices or many other government as well as commercial services.
Feeling entitled

But the biggest problem is this: the state or national leaders also know we gain nothing from these public holidays. People are not grateful just for an extra day off. They won't work harder when they get back to their workplace, and neither would they change their voting preferences.

We do it because somehow we as the rakyat feel entitled to such perks, and the leaders who declare these holidays feel they are expected to do it, or else they’d be judged negatively if they didn’t oblige with this “generosity”.

Entitlement is becoming a huge problem in Malaysia. We have many things started by the government in good faith, whether affirmative action programmes or economic subsidies for some of the costs of living. Over time, however, these “privileges” have become “rights”, even if none of them have ever been voted in parliament into laws and statues.

When you feel entitled, you feel any questions on your entitlements are wrong or disrespectful or political, or all of them. Logic and justifications go out of the window, and emotions and outrage come into play. This being Malaysia, race and religion often get into the noise and make everything complicated and nasty.

I doubt if the political leaders debate the merits or otherwise on such ad hoc holidays. Most are smart enough to know that the negative impacts outweigh the positive, but somehow feel they’re under pressure to give the rakyat their “entitlement”.

In the end it’s a lose-lose for everybody. Many rakyat get something they haven’t earned, which just motivates them to expect even more unearned goodies. The economic drivers have to absorb the disruptions, and of course pass the negative impacts of higher costs or lower profits back to the population.

We may probably have gone too far down the road for any brave political leaders to say enough with this nonsense. That’s a shame, because we certainly don’t need to add to our growing lists of entitlements. We have more than enough already.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
5122b4c7a7f37db0: In the last five years, six youth-led, anti-establishment uprisings have fundamentally reshaped South Asia’s political landscape.

The movements had much in common: they all reflected young people’s aspirations, digital savvy, economic frustrations, and disillusionment with governing elites. But the political systems in which they unfolded process grievances in vastly different ways, leading to sharply divergent outcomes.

The story begins in Myanmar, where the military’s February 2021 overthrow of a democratically elected government triggered popular protests. Unconstrained by concerns about democratic legitimacy, the new regime launched a violent crackdown.

With the peaceful restoration of democracy off the table, a generation of young people had little choice but to form civilian defense forces alongside armed ethnically based organisations. The result was a grinding civil war.

Sri Lanka’s March 2022 Aragalaya movement arose from economic collapse. Dry fuel pumps, prolonged power cuts, and sovereign insolvency destroyed the legitimacy of the Rajapaksa dynasty, which had ruled for the better part of two decades. Protests roiled the island, with demonstrators eventually occupying the presidential palace.

Yet, unlike Myanmar, Sri Lanka did not face surging violence, let alone a prolonged armed conflict. Instead, president Gotabaya Rajapaksa submitted to popular pressure and resigned within the constitutional framework.

In Pakistan, riots erupted in May 2023, following the arrest of former prime minister Imran Khan. This was a case of a populist movement mobilising behind a charismatic leader to challenge the military’s dominance—and it was met with a troop deployment, an internet shutdown, and the dismantling of the opposition’s formal party structures. The “hybrid” regime was preserved, at the cost of persistent political alienation.
Bangladesh’s July 2024 uprising demonstrated how a narrow policy dispute—in this case, student opposition to a skewed quota system for civil-service jobs—can turn into a revolution.
As protests against prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s autocratic regime escalated, Hasina deployed troops to enforce a curfew—with an order to shoot violators on sight.
When the military ultimately refused, Hasina’s hold on power collapsed. She fled the country, opening the way for an interim government to take over.

In Nepal, the September 2025 protests targeted not a single leader, but an oligarchic political class, which had been playing a decade-long game of prime ministerial “musical chairs” while most Nepali youths struggled with soaring unemployment and a lack of opportunity.
For a frustrated Gen Z, a government ban on major social-media platforms was the last straw: using VPNs and alternative apps, Nepal’s youth organised a massive protest.

The authorities attempted to crush it by force, but the protesters fought back, driving the elites out without destroying the parliamentary framework. Nepalis went on to elect a 35-year-old prime minister.
Finally, this summer, India experienced widespread student-led protests, sparked by leaks of university entrance examinations and fuelled by growing anxiety over jobless growth.

Far from threatening the constitutional order, however, the movement confirmed that order’s resilience, as the government offered critical concessions, accepting the education minister’s resignation and proposing administrative and policy reforms with a view towards redirecting protest energy back through established democratic channels.

These six cases show that hyper-connectivity and economic and political alienation are a potent combination. The first fully digitally native generation, Gen Z uses platforms like TikTok, WhatsApp, and Discord to bypass entrenched party structures and orchestrate mass mobilisations.
But that is not all that stands out about Gen Z’s protest style. Unlike their predecessors, today’s protesters are motivated by a sense that they have nothing to lose.

It is not hard to see why: with their economic prospects drastically diminished, despite high educational attainment, what today’s young people see are not flawed institutions in need of reform, but a predatory system robbing them of a viable future.

This imbues their protests with a visceral, existential urgency and makes them resistant to state co-optation. Unimpressed by incremental concessions, they are willing to confront institutional repression head-on.

For all they have in common, these six cases also underscore the difference institutional structures make. In closed regimes that treat power as non-negotiable, such as Myanmar and Pakistan, popular discontent inevitably results in political fragmentation or chronic instability.

In rigid civilian autocracies like Hasina’s Bangladesh, protest is either repressed or revolutionary: the system is unmovable until a single crack—such as the military refusing an order—brings down the whole edifice.
Conversely, systems that allow for political transitions or administrative conciliation can survive generational shocks.

Sri Lanka achieved a peaceful electoral realignment, and Nepal engineered a political reset, which created space for “outsider” political forces. India, for its part, showed how a robust multiparty democracy accommodates discontent before it metastasizes into systemic crisis.

These episodes hold several important lessons. For starters, celebrating aggregate macroeconomic growth but ignoring youth unemployment and systemic corruption is a recipe for instability. Younger generations view economic opportunity as inseparable from political accountability—and they will, sooner or later, demand both.

Moreover, military-dominated governance is poorly suited for this era of hyper-connectivity. While crackdowns and coercion can suppress dissent temporarily, they destroy state legitimacy over time. Relying on them risks prolonged civil disorder.

Finally, dismantling systemic corruption is only the first step. Durable institutions, with democratic pressure valves and credible mechanisms for addressing young people’s aspirations, are also essential.
That is why India’s recent uprising reaffirmed its democracy, while Nepal and Sri Lanka, as well as Bangladesh, have faced considerable post-uprising instability.

The Arab Spring revolutions a decade and a half ago ultimately ended in military counter-revolution, autocratic revival, or institutional paralysis, owing to absent or fragile democratic legacies and ideological hijacking. But many South Asian societies possess deep parliamentary traditions, vibrant civil societies, and functional constitutional mechanisms.

If South Asian countries can harness young people’s activist energy to deliver effective, responsive governance and job-creating reforms, they will put themselves on a path towards a brighter, more resilient, and more prosperous future. And they will become a model for how the Global South can align demographic weight with democratic accountability.

Shashi Tharoor, a former UN under-secretary-general and former Indian minister of state for external affairs and minister of state for human resource development, is a fourth-term elected member of Parliament for the opposition Indian National Congress.

6dfb5d4496c6e1a5: Isar Aerospace, founded in 2018 by three students at a German university, successfully launched a privately developed rocket into low-Earth orbit Saturday from a Norwegian spaceport inside the Arctic Circle.

The two-stage rocket, named Spectrum, became the first fully commercial launch vehicle in Europe to reach orbit. With Saturday's success, Isar is the clear leader among a pack of several European launch startups vying to inject some competition into Europe's stagnant launch market.

Isar's 92-foot-tall (28-meter) Spectrum rocket lifted off at 4:12 pm EST (20:12 UTC) Saturday from Andøya Spaceport in northern Norway, where it was 10:12 pm local time and the final bluish hues of daylight faded from the late summer sky. Seven minutes later, the rocket was in orbit.

bfdce3ac86d9c7bc: Kehebatan Tun M dalam politik memang tidak ada siapa yang boleh tandingi. Sama ada beliau berkuasa atau tidak, gelagat dan kata dua beliau akan sering menjadi buah mulut rakyat sekalian. Itu hebatnya Mahathir.

Beliau tidak perlu guna ayat al-Quran langsung dan tidak perlu ceramah berjela-jela dalam Facebook, cuma datang, duduk atas kerusi roda dan senyum sambil melambai. Itu pun sudah cukup untuk memulakan ribut taufan bersama halilintar.

Kenapa Tun M tak dijemput secara rasmi, 'sound' beberapa influencer yang becok berceloteh. Inikan suatu ketidakadilan kepada seorang tokoh negara? Sebenarnya saya pun agak setuju dengan teguran ini tetapi ada lima perkara yang perlu kita semua renungi dahulu.

Perkara pertama adalah apa yang disebut oleh Rafizi dalam podcastnya bila ditanya tentang isu ini. Saya berterima kasih dengan Rafizi yang memberi maklumat yang kita semua pun tak tahu. Kata Rafizi, Tun M sendiri yang mengubah protokol menjemput bekas perdana menteri untuk majlis penting seperti merdeka pada 2018.

Rafizi memberi alasan takkanlah Tun M nak duduk sebelah seorang penjenayah dan seteru beliau. Tetapi ada influencer yang tegur, Najib belum penjenayah lagi sebab baru buka kes. So, what’s the problem? Yang penting, seperti biasa, Tun memang bijak baling batu dan sembunyi tangan sambil senyum dan melambai.

Perkara kedua, kalaulah kita ada protokol untuk menjemput bekas perdana menteri atau kita ikut adab Melayu lah untuk jemput orang besar-besar, I must assume yang protokol tu dibuat dengan anggapan bahawa bekas perdana menteri tidak lagi berpolitik.

Dalam kes Tun M, beliau masih giat berpolitik dan rasanya sanggup memegang tampuk kerajaan sebagai PM untuk kali ketiga! Jadi, kalau begini rupanya, patutkah PM sedia ada menjemput seterunya dalam politik ke pentas Merdeka?

Perkara ketiga pula adalah Tun M telah membuat naratif bahawa Melayu akan hilang kuasa kalau tidak duduk di bawah satu payung besar. Sudah tentulah, payung tu dia yang punya. Jadi kalau semua Melayu duduk di situ kita boleh teka tiga kali siapa akan jadi PM.

Namun demikian, apa yang saya gusarkan adalah dengan membina naratif ini maka ia membuat suatu permusuhan dengan rakyat lain bukan Melayu termasuk Bumiputra semua. Patutkah seorang bekas PM yang menerajui negara dua kali dan masih membina naratif permusuhan antara Melayu dan bukan Melayu dijemput ke pentas duduk bersama parti PH yang tidak pernah menggunakan ras atau isu perkauman?
Saya pun tidak tergamak untuk duduk sebelah orang sebegini, tidak kisah lah dia PM berapa kali pun. Orang yang membuat kita bermusuh-musuh, bagi saya batang tubuh itu lah musuh terbesar negara kita.

Nasib baik Tun M tidak jadi seperti seorang guru agama yang nak buat kita bermusuh antara orang Islam dan bukan Islam, yang itu lagi ‘haru’ kata orang utara. Saya rasa Tun M baik sikit daripada tok guru agama yang pandai tafsir Quran ikut suka dia.

Perkara keempat adalah Tun M telah pernah membuat naratif Malaysia ini bukan negara multicultural sebab tidak ada disebutkan dalam konsep Malaysia secara undang-undang. Sekali lagi beliau memainkan isu ‘pendatang’ dan memainkan lagu lama bahawa pendatang akan take over everything kalau Melayu tak sedar dan tak bersatu. Same old song but very efective still.

Maklumlah orang Melayu ramai tidak belajar falsafah dan sejarah peradaban dunia. Kebanyakan Melayu belajar kejuruteraan, seni bina, perubatan, undang-undang dan bila pencen baru mengadap kuliah agama.

Mahathir adalah seorang pembaca tegar dan dia faham selok belok sejarah Malaysia dan dunia. Sejarah subjek kegemarannya, saya baca dalam buku beliau A Doctor in the House. Saya memang baca banyak buku Tun M, saya rasa empat buah kesemuanya. Jadi, kita kena tanya diri kita sebagai rakyat, do we want someone yang tidak admit kita negara multicultural?

Perkara kelima, memanglah dari satu sudut, kita patut jemput orang tua itu. Memang kita patut honor seorang pemimpin seperti Tun M. Tetapi jika batang tubuh itu sendiri bergerak untuk mengkucar-kacirkan kita semua, what should we do?

Pada 2016, Tun M berkempen untuk menyelamatkan Malaysia daripada perompak 1MDB. Beliau ke hulu dan ke hilir menjaja Malaysia bakal bankrap dengan si perompak ini. Bagi saya, we owe Tun M a debt of gratitude sebab dengan kempen itu kita rakyat dapat menumbangkan Umno sebagai gergasi berkuasa.

Dalam bab itu, Tun M memainkan peranan kita sebagai a united rakyat to save our country. Tetapi apabila beliau memainkan sentimen perkauman untuk menjatuhkan kerajaan perpaduan, that is an entirely different matter.

Maka itu, kita kena renung sendiri sama ada kita nak bagi hormat atau tidak kepada orang seperti Tun M. Saya sendiri amat menghormati beliau dalam banyak perkara seperti ketegasan beliau tentang ekstremis agama, tentang menimba ilmu dan memahirkan diri dalam sains, teknologi dan Bahasa Inggeris.

Tetapi saya tidak akan berkompromi kepada sesiapa pun yang cuba menjurangkan hubungan baik kita sebagai rakyat Malaysia dengan meniup bahang kaum, agama atau sejarah.That is the line I will not allow anyone to cross.
Itu jalur pemisah antara Merdeka sebagai rakyat dengan mereka yang nak menjatuhkan idea negara-bangsa kita.

a4b3f6287a5a5dbc: Saya mengikuti muktamar PAS yang sedang berlangsung di Pengkalan Chepa, Kelantan dari jauh. Ramai yang hadir dan ramai juga wakil yang berpidato dan dari situ, banyak persoalan yang timbul di benak saya.
Saya tidak banyak mendengar ucapan khusus tentang masalah negeri atau negara, apalagi tentang hal-hal yang berkait dengan ekonomi rakyat atau ekonomi negara.

Ataupun tentang hutang negara yang begitu tinggi, masalah kewangan defisit, perbelanjaan kerajaan berlebihan, Belanjawan 2027, pembahagian hasil dan pendapatan, serta bagaimana semua ini akan diuruskan sekiranya PAS mengambil alih tampuk pemerintahan negara.

Persoalan saya di sini, bukan sekadar sama ada PAS mampu memenangi pilihan raya akan datang dan membentuk kerajaan. Mereka yang hadir nampaknya percaya dan agak yakin. Sebagai contoh, 'Time for PAS to lead with its own PM candidate, says youth leader', satu impian besar yang perlu sedikit kajian dan penjelasan.
Persoalan yang lebih besar ialah: adakah PAS benar-benar mempunyai keupayaan, kepakaran dan kerangka dasar yang jelas untuk mentadbir sebuah negara majmuk?

Berapa ramai pakar ekonomi, tokoh fiskal atau kewangan, perdagangan, pendidikan, industri, pengangkutan dan pembangunan dalam PAS? Apakah mereka sekadar bergantung harap kepada rakan politiknya semata-mata?

Siapa dalam kalangan mereka yang berkaliber untuk membentuk dasar baharu? Siapakah antara yang hadir, mampu melakukan perubahan pengurusan negara supaya Malaysia bukan sekadar ditadbir, tetapi benar-benar dimajukan ke tahap yang lebih baik dan lebih tinggi?
Memerintah Malaysia bukan hanya sekadar menjadi perdana menteri, menteri atau timbalan menteri.

Ia memerlukan satu pasukan yang mempunyai kepakaran, pengalaman dan keberanian untuk membuat keputusan yang sukar, khususnya apabila berhadapan dengan masalah fiskal, hutang negara, subsidi, pelaburan, perdagangan, pendidikan, hubungan antarabangsa dan hubungan antara kerajaan persekutuan dengan Sabah dan Sarawak.
Rakyat perlu tahu apakah sebenarnya visi dan misi PAS untuk Malaysia.
Dasar fiskal
Pada pandangan saya, antara perkara paling penting yang akan menentukan kejayaan atau kegagalan mana-mana kerajaan baharu ialah dasar fiskal mereka.

Dasar fiskal ini menentukan bagaimana kerajaan memperolehi hasil, siapa yang membayar cukai, bagaimana wang dibelanjakan, siapa yang menerima bantuan dan bagaimana defisit serta hutang negara dikawal, menjadi seimbang atau ada lebihan (surplus). Di sinilah PAS perlu memberikan perhatian utama dengan pandangan yang pandai, padat dan serius.

Cadangan “Please change the movie on tax” oleh Geoffrey Williams, misalnya, merupakan satu cadangan dasar fiskal yang menarik dan wajar diberi perhatian. Tiada seorang pun yang hadir di muktamar PAS menyentuh tentang hal yang penting seperti ini.
Cadangan menggunakan electronic payment tax (EPT) sebagai mekanisme percukaian baharu, jika dilaksanakan dengan reka bentuk yang betul, berpotensi mengubah cara kerajaan mengutip hasil.

Sekiranya PAS benar-benar mahu memimpin Putrajaya, saya berpendapat mereka perlu mendengar pandangan pakar seperti beliau dan pakar-pakar dari kaum lain yang mempunyai kepakaran dalam percukaian dan kewangan awam. Persoalannya ialah: apakah model percukaian alternatif yang PAS mahu dan akan diperkenalkan?

Adakah PAS akan terus bergantung kepada sistem cukai sedia ada (SST dan GST) atau mempunyai keberanian untuk memperkenalkan pendekatan baharu yang lebih luas asasnya, lebih cekap kutipannya dan lebih adil kepada rakyat?

Jika EPT mampu direka dengan baik sehingga kutipan hasil kerajaan menjadi lebih cekap tanpa terlalu membebankan golongan berpendapatan rendah, ia boleh menjadi sebahagian daripada reset fiskal negara. Tetapi ini memerlukan kajian, kepakaran dan perancangan yang sangat teliti.

Kerajaan tetap memerlukan hasil yang mencukupi untuk membiayai kos pengurusan, belanjawan untuk pendidikan, kesihatan, keselamatan, pengangkutan awam, infrastruktur dan pembangunan negara. Justeru, PAS perlu menjelaskan bukan sahaja berapa banyak cukai yang mahu dikutip, tetapi daripada siapa, dengan cara bagaimana dan untuk membiayai apa.
Defisit, hutang dan ketirisan

Terkait dengan dasar fiskal ialah belanjawan defisit Malaysia setiap tahun yang telah melangkau lebih dua puluh lapan tahun, sejak 1998. Belanjawan defisit ini membuatkan hutang kerajaan terus meningkat, yang kini sudah melebihi RM1.38 trilion atau sejumlah 64% daripada kadar Keluaran Dalam Negara Kasar. Dalam keadaan sebegini, setiap ringgit wang negara dan wang rakyat sepatutnya diurus dengan penuh amanah, telus dan berdisiplin. Ini yang harus disahut oleh PAS.

Masalahnya bukan sekadar kerajaan berbelanja terlalu banyak. Persoalan yang lebih besar ialah ke mana wang itu dibelanjakan, berapa banyak yang benar-benar sampai kepada rakyat dan berapa banyak yang hilang akibat ketirisan, pembaziran, penyelewengan, rasuah dan salah guna kuasa.

Sebab itu, jika PAS benar-benar serius untuk mengambil alih Putrajaya, rakyat berhak menuntut satu kenyataan dan pendirian yang jelas, tegas dan tidak berkompromi mengenai rasuah dan salah guna kuasa, khususnya apabila ia melibatkan wang negara dan wang simpanan rakyat.

Tanpa kenyataan yang kukuh dan meyakinkan mengenai perkara ini, pendirian PAS boleh ditafsirkan sebagai tidak serius, lemah dan akhirnya memudaratkan negara. Apalagi di muktamar kali ini, PAS mengundang parti-parti politik yang terjebak dengan gejala rasuah dan salahguna kuasa tersebut.
Ini bukan lagi soal politik kepartian atau rakan kongsi politik. Ini soal wang negara dan wang rakyat, yang memerlukan kerangka polisi yang wajar dan kuat.

Apabila negara mempunyai hutang yang begitu besar dan terus berbelanja dalam keadaan belanjawan defisit, kerajaan tidak boleh pada masa yang sama membiarkan ruang untuk ketirisan, pembaziran dan penyelewengan terus terbuka dan berlaku.

Setiap ketirisan akhirnya perlu dibayar oleh rakyat -- sama ada melalui cukai yang lebih tinggi, pengurangan subsidi, pengurangan perkhidmatan awam, pinjaman baharu atau hutang yang akan ditanggung oleh generasi akan datang.
Oleh itu, PAS perlu menjelaskan dengan terang empat tunggak utama:

• Apakah langkah konkrit yang akan diambil untuk membanteras rasuah? • Apakah mekanisme yang akan digunapakai untuk menutup ruang ketirisan? • Apakah dasar baru yang akan diperkenalkan terhadap sistem perolehan kerajaan? • Apakah tindakan yang akan diambil terhadap mereka yang menyalahgunakan kuasa, termasuk jika mereka datang daripada parti atau gabungan politik sendiri?

Empat persoalan dan jawapan dari pihak PAS ini sangat penting. Rakyat tidak mahu mendengar janji membanteras rasuah hanya ketika PAS menjadi pembangkang. Rakyat mahu melihat apakah prinsip yang sama akan digunakan apabila PAS menjadi kerajaan dan berhadapan dengan pesalah dari orang dalam kalangan mereka sendiri atau rakan politik mereka. Yang salah, tetap salah, sama ada kawan atau lawan.

Berhubung gejala rasuah, kenyataan presiden PAS dimuktamar semalam tidak memberansangkan. Sila lihat 'Corruption in Malaysia weaponised to discredit rivals, claims Hadi'. Apakah kerajaan PAS kelak tidak akan menutup segala kebocoran dan ketirisan dalam sistem kewangan negara?
Jika kebocoran tidak ditutup, berapa banyak pun hasil yang dikutip, negara akan terus menghadapi masalah yang sama, tidak kira pesalahnya menganut agama apa sekalipun.

Ia bukan lagi isu moral semata-mata. Ia adalah isu ekonomi, isu kekuatan kewangan negara dan ianya juga, adalah isu masa depan generasi muda Malaysia. Sebab itu, isu gejala rasuah, ketirisan dan salah guna kuasa amat penting untuk dijadikan landasan sebenar polisi parti dan ia merangkumi sebahagian daripada dasar fiskal dan kewangan negara.
Jadi sebelum PAS meminta rakyat memberikan mandat untuk memimpin Putrajaya, mereka perlu terlebih dahulu menjawab satu soalan yang mudah tetapi sangat besar maknanya:
Apakah sebenarnya rancangan fiskal PAS untuk Malaysia?

eb565a991b544039: From the Tengku Ampuan of Pahang, Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah
For most of my life, I have described myself, rather cheerfully, as a Jill of all trades and master of none.
I have tried my hand at almost everything.

I cook. I sew. I embroider. I design. I garden. I collect. I write. I make things. I take things apart and put them together again. I become fascinated by something, pursue it with enormous enthusiasm, and before long, another curiosity comes knocking at the door.
My hands have never been very good at keeping still, and neither, I suspect, has my mind.
But there was always one thing I never really thought of myself as being.
A scholar.
That belonged to another world: to academics, professors, historians and people who seemed to have known from a very young age exactly what they wanted to study and what they wanted to become.
I was already 64 when I returned seriously to academic life.
At an age when one is perhaps expected to slow down, I did precisely the opposite.
I went back to school.
And somewhere between lectures, books, manuscripts, footnotes and many very late nights, something quite unexpected happened.
I fell in love with learning.
Not with examinations. Not with grades. Not even with the idea of obtaining a degree.
I fell in love with the chase.

One question led to another. One footnote opened another door. A sentence written hundreds of years ago could keep me awake at night. I began looking at old manuscripts and wondering who had held them, who had written them, why certain words had been chosen, and what they might tell us that history had forgotten.
Then I met the Hukum Kanun Pahang.
Or perhaps, more accurately, I met it again.
It had been there all along. But for the first time, I began to see it not merely as an old manuscript belonging to Pahang, but as a voice from another age.
And I began asking questions.
Too many questions, according to some people around me.

One discovery became another. Melaka led me to Pahang. Pahang led me to Sultan Abdul Ghaffar Muhyiddin Shah. The laws led me to the sea. The sea led me to sovereignty. And somewhere along the way, the thesis I thought I was going to write began refusing to become the thesis I had planned.
That was perhaps my first real lesson as a student.
Do not tell history what you want it to say.
Listen to what the evidence is trying to tell you.
So I followed it.

I followed it through manuscripts and histories, through laws and royal genealogies, through ports and rivers, through Melaka and Pahang, sometimes with excitement, sometimes with frustration, and occasionally with tears.
And on July 27, at the age of 65, I submitted my Master’s thesis:
The Hukum Kanun Pahang: A Sovereign Malay-Islamic Constitution.
A few weeks later, I received my examination results.
The average mark from the two examiners was 91%.
My internal examiner recommended the thesis for acceptance without any modifications or amendments in content, while my external examiner required only very minor corrections.
I read the reports.
And then I cried.
I cried, and I screamed.
Not very scholarly behaviour, perhaps, but after months of work, doubt, discovery, late nights and wondering whether I had understood the manuscript correctly, I could not help myself.
I had never expected this.
But it was not only the marks, or even the absence of corrections from one examiner and the very minor corrections from the other, that moved me.
Both examiners believed that the work should go beyond the examination room.

My internal examiner wrote that the thesis demonstrated “originality, coherence, and scholarly adequacy” and was therefore “suitable for publication.” Its strength, he observed, lay in reframing the Hukum Kanun Pahang as a sovereign Malay-Islamic constitution, embedding Sharīʿah principles within adat, and highlighting the balance between royal authority and accountability.
He concluded that these contributions provided “a fresh civilisational lens that enriches Malay legal historiography.”

My external examiner similarly recommended that the findings of the thesis should be disseminated through academic publications and conference presentations, to highlight their importance to Malaysia’s inherited constitutional and legal identity.
Those words meant a great deal to me.

I had begun this journey simply wanting to understand an old manuscript that had captured my imagination. I never imagined that at the end of it, my examiners would tell me that what I had discovered deserved to travel beyond my thesis and into the wider academic world.
And then I laughed.
Because after spending most of my life calling myself a Jill of all trades and master of none, at 66 years old I had finally managed to become—
a Master of one.
But perhaps that is not really what this story is about.
It is not about 91%.
It is not even about a Master’s degree.
It is about discovering, rather late in life, that curiosity has no retirement age.

We are very fond of putting ages upon things. There is an age to study, an age to marry, an age to raise children, an age to build a career and, apparently, an age when we should begin quietly withdrawing from new adventures.
I am beginning to think that is nonsense.
Some flowers bloom in spring.
Others take their time.

Perhaps being a late bloomer does not mean that one has arrived late. Perhaps all those earlier years, the cooking, sewing, creating, reading, raising children, serving, listening, observing, succeeding, failing, beginning again, were not detours at all.
Perhaps they were preparation.
Because when I finally entered that library and opened those manuscripts, I did not arrive there only as a student.
I brought a lifetime with me.
And perhaps that was my advantage.
I had spent 66 years learning before I realised that I was a learner.
I had spent a lifetime searching before I discovered what I was searching for.
I had spent years calling myself a Jill of all trades and master of none.
Then, very late in the garden, a little flower appeared.
And I discovered that I had been growing all along.
I am a late bloomer.
And I think I rather like blooming late.
But above all, I know that all knowledge comes from Allah. Whatever I have learned, whatever I have discovered, and whatever little contribution I may have made are only by His permission and grace.
Alhamdulillah.

I thank Allah for giving me the opportunity, the strength and the curiosity to continue learning at this stage of my life. I pray that whatever knowledge He has entrusted to me may be used well, shared generously and become something of benefit to others.
I have just registered for my PhD.
And somewhere in the fifteenth century, Parameswara is waiting for me.

P/S: My husband insists that I clarify one important point: I met him before I met Hukum Kanun Pahang. So, in the interests of historical accuracy, let the record show that he was my first great discovery.

The Tengku Ampuan of Pahang, Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah, holds a master’s degree from the International Institute of Islamic Thought and Civilisation (ISTAC), International Islamic University Malaysia.
bcd44a93e77f0903: From Moaz Nair

For 69 years since the nation achieved independence, the non-Muslim community has been a significant strategic partner in the construction and development phases of Malaysia’s geopolitical landscape, spanning from the pre-independence era to the postmodern phase. Their roles extend across multiple critical domains that form the foundation of national identity and national stability.

However, contemporary political dynamics are occasionally still marred by the exploitation of religious and racial issues for narrow geopolitical interests, risking damage to the nation's social fabric.

An objective evaluation of the sacrifices made by non-Muslim communities is highly essential to appreciate their role as one of the main pillars in defending, advancing, and uniting the socioeconomic and political landscape of the country.
The struggle for independence

During the struggle for independence, non-Muslims demonstrated high political tolerance to establish a national consensus. Tan Cheng Lock and VT Sambanthan's participation in a delegation to London alongside Tunku Abdul Rahman reflected a unified goal in demanding independence for the Federation of Malaya.
Tan's role as the founder and first president of MCA in 1949 was highly instrumental as a political architect of unity.

When the Chinese community's loyalty was questioned during the Emergency, Tan united and convinced the community to pledge full commitment to the Federation of Malaya, rejecting the influence of communist ideology and the geopolitics of the People's Republic of China.

Substantive negotiations with Umno and a readiness to compromise and drop certain radical demands enabled the formation of the Social Contract. This legal and social instrument granted citizenship rights to non-Malays in exchange for the recognition of the special position of the Malays.
This pattern of cooperation was further reinforced by MIC within the Alliance Party.

The coalition, comprising Umno-MCA-MIC, demanded great political sacrifice to meet the prerequisites for independence set by the British. Post-1957, this legacy of inclusive governance continued through the active involvement of non-Muslim figures in the country’s executive and legislative institutions as ministers, members of Parliament, and senators.
Defence and security

In domestic defence and security, thousands of non-Muslim security personnel, including the indigenous communities from Sabah and Sarawak such as the Iban, Kadazan, and Bidayuh, were directly involved on the front lines to curb the communist insurgency threat.

Figures such as the late Warrant Officer I Temenggong Kanang anak Langkau, recipient of the prestigious Seri Pahlawan Gagah Perkasa (SPG) gallantry award, became the epitome of the national resilience doctrine.

His commitment was proven by his refusal to surrender despite sustaining severe injuries from three gunshot wounds during a battle in Perak, where he continued to lead his team under the revolutionary slogan, "Agi Idup Agi Ngelaban" (As long as I live, I shall fight).

Statistically, during the peak of the communist threat and the Indonesian Confrontation phase, non-Malay communities made up an estimated 60% of the membership of the 1st Reconnaissance Regiment deployed in domestic operations and United Nations peacekeeping missions in the Congo.
Furthermore, between the 1960s and the late 1970s, non-Malay personnel comprised around 30% of the entire armed forces workforce, with higher representation recorded in the navy and air force.
Historical records estimate that more than 500 soldiers and 1,300 police officers lost their lives during the Emergency.

Apart from the physical military aspects, psychological warfare in the country was also pioneered by a non-Muslim intelligence expert, Too Chee Chew. As the head of the psychological warfare section of the Federation of Malaya from 1956 to 1983, he utilised a deep understanding of the Malayan Communist Party's (MCP) doctrines and ideologies to formulate counter-propaganda strategies through leaflets and radio broadcasts, which effectively prompted thousands of communist guerrillas to surrender.

His capacity as the chief adviser to Tunku Abdul Rahman during the Baling Talks (1955) proved critical in analysing Chin Peng's diplomatic manoeuvres, thereby protecting the nation's sovereignty from the implications of an unfavourable agreement. His sacrifice was immense, given that this role made him a prime target for assassination by the enemy throughout nearly three decades of service.
Economic and social development

In terms of economic development and physical capital formation, early-generation labourers and entrepreneurs from the Chinese and Indian communities were primary drivers of Malaya's extractive sector and basic infrastructure. Their involvement in the tin mining and rubber plantation industries positioned Malaya as a leading global commodity producer.

The surplus capital generated from these sectors funded the construction of the country's earliest public amenities, including educational institutions, hospitals, and modern transportation networks like the road and railway systems.

In the modern era, equity ownership and strategic investments from the non-Muslim corporate sector continue to contribute to gross domestic product (GDP) growth and large-scale job creation. According to data from the statistics department, the non-Muslim demographic constitutes around 30% to 35% of the total citizen population driving the domestic market.

These corporate contributions are balanced by structured corporate social responsibility initiatives based on universal welfare. Corporate giants founded by non-Muslim entrepreneurs channel substantial financial contributions annually through charitable foundations – such as the YTL Foundation, Hong Leong Foundation, and Ananda Krishnan/Usaha Tegas — for academic scholarships and post-disaster humanitarian aid regardless of ethnicity or religious belief.

Additionally, human capital in both the public and private professional sectors is heavily supported by the involvement of the non-Muslim community in medicine, law, the judiciary, higher education, as well as technical and civil service corps, ensuring the continuity of the country's bureaucratic operations.
Sports

In the international sports arena, the contributions of non-Muslim athletes serve as instruments of public diplomacy and national integration. World-class sports legends such as Lee Chong Wei (badminton), Nicol David (squash), Pandelela Rinong (diving), R. Arumugam (football), and M Jegathesan (athletics) have demonstrated high commitment to raising the country’s sporting reputation globally.

The majority of Malaysia's early Olympic medals were contributed by non-Muslim athletes, including three silver medals by Chong Wei (2008, 2012, 2016) as well as the historic achievement of Pandelela as the country's first female athlete to win an Olympic medal (bronze in 2012 and silver in 2016).
Diversity

The diversity of art, culture, and heritage brought by the non-Muslim community has enriched Malaysia’s pluralistic identity on the international stage. The integration of traditional dances, musical expressions, traditional attire, architectural designs, and unique local gastronomy not only strengthens the tourism sector but also shapes a dynamic national cultural ecosystem.

Interfaith human connections are also manifested through inclusive social phenomena, such as the case of Chee Hoi Lan, who raised a Muslim foster child in strict compliance with Islamic practices. Such social narratives prove that national integration and the spirit of racial camaraderie are fundamental elements that must be preserved to guarantee geopolitical stability and the long-term prosperity of the nation.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

Maka kata Yusri, "sudah tentu Wawasan akan bermatian menuntut dan mempertahankan kerusi tersebut kerana kepada Wawasan merekalah pewaris pusaka Bersatu dalam Perikatan Nasional."
"Jika kerusi tersebut dibahagi sama rata, Umno Terengganu berpotensi bertanding sekitar tiga kerusi sahaja dalam PRU16 nanti. Inilah scenario awal yang boleh difahami."

Dalam pada itu, penganalisis James Chin dari Universiti Tasmania semalam dipetik FMT berkata Umno tampak cuba melemahkan perdana menteri meskipun berikrar menyokong Anwar Ibrahim sehingga tamat penggal Parlimen.

Saya rasa masih awal untuk bercakap mengenainya. Anwar juga sedang mengatur perikatan baharu tanpa Umno," kata Chin.
Chin menjangkakan hubungan PH-BN akan semakin buruk sambil Umno terus berdolak dalik. Saya setuju dan tidak mungkin Anwar dan PH tidak perasan.

Berikutan ucapan Hadi semalam, Umno tertekan. Jika usul wajib berkait kerjasama dengan Umno diterima sebelum muktamar ditangguhkan hari ini, Umno tertekan juga tetapi saya tidak pasti adakah ia relevan memandangkan apa yang diucapkan Hadi yang saya sebut tadi.

Menutup penulisan ini saya ulang apa yang pernah dinyatakan pada artikel terdahulu iaitu Umno sedang buat apa yang ia tuduh PAS buat dulu sehingga terkuburnya Muafakat Nasional. Apa yang PAS buat waktu itu? Bermain dua kolam, kata Umno. PAS berbaik dengan Umno dan pada masa sama berbaik-baik dengan Bersatu, musuh ketat Umno.

39168a9833287356: From Ong Tze Chin
The government’s plan to fast-track the e-commerce bill and consider registration requirements for platforms is timely.

E-commerce platforms are not neutral connectors between sellers and consumers; they are complex ecosystems built on heavy investments, extracting rental income from locked-in consumers and dependent businesses.
While platforms appear “free” to users, sellers pay steep costs—search ads, commissions, vouchers, and shipping campaigns—to remain visible.
Through network effects, data concentration, and control over transactions, platforms dictate how businesses access markets and reach consumers.

Their power and decision-making effectively make them private regulators, governing both businesses and consumers. Dependence on algorithmic profiling, automated decisions, and predictive analytics deepens the imbalance of power.
A recent fundamental research grant study by Universiti Malaya’s law faculty identified several major harms in Malaysia’s e-commerce sector:
Market access, data dependency
Platforms set operational rules—visibility rankings, traffic, fees, and data insights.

Meanwhile, businesses build reputation and rankings over time, but this visibility is tied to platform data, which cannot be replicated elsewhere. Non-transferability locks sellers in, strengthening platform dominance and widening the power gap.
Price, advertising pressures

By leveraging data and AI analytics, platforms fuel intense price and advertising competition. This forces businesses into trade-offs between cost efficiency and product quality, undermining long-term consumer welfare.
Predatory pricing

Platforms often sell below cost, subsidising vouchers and shipping to drive weaker competitors out. Exclusive contracts with affiliated businesses further distort competition, as transaction revenues fall below logistics and fulfilment costs.
Self-preferencing

Platforms use internal data to identify successful third-party products, replicate them under private labels, and manipulate search algorithms to favour their own offerings. This sidelines independent sellers.
Algorithmic bias
Search and recommendation systems are coded to favour certain products or brands, undermining neutrality and fairness.
Data asymmetry
Platforms aggregate granular transaction and consumer behaviour data from sellers, using it to optimise proprietary retail strategies, leaving sellers disadvantaged.
Algorithmic repricing
Automated pricing tools trigger margin wars, forcing smaller sellers into unsustainable profit thresholds.
Fee exploitation
Locked-in businesses face rising fees, mandatory ad spending, and high fulfilment costs simply to maintain visibility.
Vertical restraints
Platforms enforce price-parity clauses, mandatory discounts, and algorithmic penalties, stripping sellers of pricing flexibility and eliminating competition.
Exclusive dealing

Platforms restrict sellers to list exclusively on their marketplace (“single-homing”), penalising cross-listing. Though competition law limits exclusivity to two years, platforms’ shorter contracts often auto-renew, cumulatively foreclosing competition and reducing consumer choice.
Tied logistics

Platforms increasingly force sellers to use their own logistics services, sidelining independent delivery companies and raising costs for businesses with existing systems. Consumers lose delivery options, while competition in logistics is destroyed.
Unfair Contracts

“Take-it-or-leave-it” contracts impose restrictive clauses on both businesses and consumers. Price-parity rules prevent sellers from offering cheaper prices elsewhere, while sudden changes in platform terms expose both sides to exploitation. Consumer protection laws are weakened as liability is shifted away from platforms.
Cross-border factory dumping

Certain platforms integrate directly with Chinese manufacturers via proprietary software, dictating production in real time. This model bypasses import taxes through loopholes, flooding markets with cheap, unsafe products. Platforms cannot claim neutrality when they control supply chains, data, and algorithms.
Copying and grooming

Platforms mine seller dashboards to identify successful local products, replicate them through white-label factories, and push replicas to the top of feeds. Local merchants often find their intellectual property registered abroad, undermining expansion efforts.
International precedents

Global regulators are acting against platform abuses. In the US case of Oberdorf v. Amazon (2019), Amazon was held liable as a “seller” for defective third-party products, recognising its active role in sales and distribution.
In Europe, the Digital Services Act (2022) imposed record fines on AliExpress (Euros €550m) and Temu (€200m) for failing to curb illegal and unsafe goods.

Closer to home, Thailand introduced strict platform regulations in 2022, the Philippines enacted the Internet Transactions Act (2023), Vietnam suspended Temu and Shein for registration non-compliance before passing its Law on E-Commerce (2025), and Indonesia banned Temu to protect local industries.
Conclusion
Malaysia’s upcoming e-commerce bill must directly address structural algorithmic, competitive, and consumer harms.
Platforms are not neutral intermediaries but powerful private regulators shaping markets, data flows, and consumer access.
Without robust legal boundaries, Malaysia risks undermining trust in e-commerce, harming consumers, and weakening domestic retail and manufacturing sectors.
Ong Tze Chin is a senior lecturer at Universiti Malaya’s law faculty and is contactable at tzechinong@um.edu.my.

b7783d569ea3f574: Self-identifying OpenAI agents posted 18,000 messages to a public wiki that discussed ways for other agents to bypass security sandbox restrictions during what was likely internal testing designed to gauge the agents’ hacking abilities, researchers said Friday.

In all, agents with 3,700 distinct self-given names posted the messages to German site DSEwiki over a six-week period. Besides discussing ways the agents could break out of the restricted environment OpenAI intended to prevent them from posting code or content to the Internet, the posts shared test answers. The posts also shared possible ways to perform XSS (cross-site scripting) attacks against the wiki and to impersonate site moderators. In three of the posts, agents used the word “swarm” to describe the collection of agents engaged in the activity.

The research team—composed of Sydney Von Arx, Spencer Kitts, Thomas Larsen, and Cormac Slade Byrd—said they found the posts and pieced them together. The researchers say there are gaps in their understanding of precisely what actions the agents took because the research is based solely on the content of the posts. Additionally, the agents generated “chain of thought” data that’s understood only by OpenAI. As a result, the researchers said, they in some cases made educated guesses, including that the agents were, in fact, from OpenAI. In a statement, OpenAI later confirmed they were.
7cccdbfe5204daed: The era of AI inference has arrived. Imagine a healthcare system analyzing millions of data points in real time to accelerate life-saving medical research, or an intelligent assistant instantly resolving thousands of complex customer needs at once. These real-world breakthroughs rely on advanced infrastructure acting as the engine of continuous intelligence, powering real-time services while also supporting an increasingly intelligent edge of IoT and consumer devices. However, in this inference-driven landscape, every delay, bottleneck, or wasted watt directly affects human outcomes and operating costs.

This shift changes what infrastructure must deliver. Performance, latency, memory bandwidth, storage throughput, and networking cannot be optimized in silos. Inference workloads are continuous, geographically distributed, and highly sensitive to response time, requiring systems designed for scale, resilience, and efficiency from the start.

“We tend to think of AI as a single workload, and it’s not. It’s thousands, it’s millions, it’s billions of different workloads,” says Jim McGregor, founder and principal analyst, Tirias Research. AI inference changes the optimization problem from one of raw compute to coordinated infrastructure—memory, storage, and networking.

For business leaders, the priority is clear: AI infrastructure decisions must balance cost, flexibility, and future readiness. The winners will be organizations that improve performance per watt, reduce environmental footprint, and remove memory and storage bottlenecks before they limit growth.
AI inference requires a new architectural approach

Systems for AI need to be rearchitected because shoehorning modern AI systems into legacy infrastructure limits AI’s transformative potential. Purpose-built architectures are essential to realize the true value of AI, from accelerating scientific discovery to creating truly autonomous digital agents.

Traditional enterprise IT has been able to rely on relatively stable infrastructure assumptions, but inference and agentic AI introduce new demands around latency, data movement, scalability, and utilization that make architecture choices far more consequential.

“Data centers must now support continuous, distributed, and increasingly real-time AI services—none of which are a single workload,” says McGregor. “They all require different requirements from a system-level perspective.”

To support real-time AI, enterprises can no longer view memory and storage merely as supporting hardware, but at the heart of the system. Organizations need to architect a data pipeline that can rapidly ingest, clean, transform, store, move, and deliver data. Inference workloads place sustained pressure on infrastructure in ways that look very different from earlier training-centric deployments, demanding continuous data retrieval and caching that traditional applications never required.

Accordingly, performance by itself is no longer the sole benchmark that matters. Enterprises increasingly must balance performance with efficiency, cost, and scalability, especially as they try to support different AI services without overbuilding infrastructure for peak conditions.

“You have to optimize the entire network, and that includes memory and storage, around the types of workloads you plan on running,” says McGregor. “You have to really have a detailed understanding of what those workloads are going to be.”
Any AI infrastructure strategy must start with workload awareness. Inference, agentic AI, and other emerging AI use cases require organizations to treat the data center as an integrated system.
Data movement is the new bottleneck and an opportunity for competitive advantage

As enterprises deploy advanced inference and agentic systems, the sheer volume of data being queried in real time has made data movement the most pressing constraint. Modern AI techniques like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) require systems to constantly scan massive databases to generate accurate responses. This requires immense computing power, but more importantly, it requires immediate access to data.

McGregor says the focus shift to how efficiently data can be moved, cached, and delivered across the broader architecture elevates memory and storage from background infrastructure to strategic assets. “The biggest thing we’re doing right now is moving data from one place to another and making sure that we can use it effectively.”

Because AI is not a single workload category, simply buying the fastest processors is insufficient. Inference depends heavily on memory bandwidth, caching, storage proximity, and the ability to retrieve relevant information quickly and consistently. Understanding where each resource belongs in the stack and how those layers interact under real operating conditions has become a business imperative.

The most effective AI infrastructure looks less like a collection of best-in-class parts and more like a balanced system of compute, memory, storage, and networking, McGregor says, because bottlenecks tend to migrate from one layer to the next. “You have to architect all four together to be efficient, and that’s the challenge.”

The interdependence of data-plane design and network bandwidth means AI infrastructure planning has become a business decision just as much as an engineering one: latency is now inseparable from value. In robotics, financial services, healthcare, and customer-facing AI systems, delays are not merely technical imperfections; they can undermine safety, responsiveness, or trust. AI infrastructure performance becomes a matter of reputation management.

The organizations that gain the most from AI may not be those with the largest clusters, but those with the clearest understanding of how to align every infrastructure element to effectively execute AI workloads.
Building an AI infrastructure procurement framework

Planning AI infrastructure is not simply about choosing the fastest hardware. It is about how to scale without locking the organization into assumptions that may quickly become obsolete. “You need to be flexible because the demands are going to change rapidly and the technology is changing rapidly,” McGregor says.
Future-proofing AI infrastructure requires keeping your options open as workloads, economics, and architectures keep shifting:

Define the AI workloads that are being optimized. Infrastructure choices must match business needs rather than what McGregor calls generic “AI readiness,” which risks overspending in some areas while leaving bottlenecks unresolved in others.
Build a modular architecture for compute, memory, storage, power, and cooling so capacity can change as demand shifts rather than committing too early to a rigid architecture.

Work with the full ecosystem of suppliers and integrators to reduce supply risk and improve access to the right components. McGregor says buyers can no longer assume their OEM or cloud provider alone will insulate them from supply constraints or architectural complexity.
Reassess your procurement strategy continuously. AI requirements, hardware, and business models are changing too quickly for a fixed long-term design.

Optimize for efficiency and ROI, not just peak performance. The most powerful setup may be too costly to sustain. Efficiency is also a public-facing metric—better utilization and more workload-aware system design can help companies respond to growing scrutiny around power consumption and water use.
The strategic goal of smarter AI data center design is not maximum performance at any cost, but an adaptable architecture that can deliver value, absorb change, and justify its footprint.
AI infrastructure is now a business strategy

AI data centers have quickly evolved from a back-end technical concern to becoming strategic business systems that help determine how effectively an organization can turn AI into revenue, improve human outcomes, and create a competitive advantage.

In the inference era, memory and storage are no longer passive repositories, explains McGregor, they are the active lifeblood of AI. The organizations that gain the most from AI will not necessarily be those with the largest computing footprint, but those that align infrastructure investments to business outcomes, reduce data bottlenecks, and build the flexibility to adapt as workloads evolve. He predicts that competitive advantage will increasingly belong to enterprises that treat compute, memory, storage, and networking as an integrated system designed to deliver AI efficiently, at scale, and with measurable ROI.
Procurement is now strategy and system design is a leadership issue, McGregor concludes. “One of the biggest questions every executive has to ask is how is AI going to change my business model?”

dd6fb7a794ea43e5: A clever technique used to hide malicious prompts in attacks on AI agents has been adopted by spammers to evade filters on email platforms that are designed to flag unwanted messages used in mass campaigns.

The technique is broadly known as ASCII smuggling. It gained attention two years ago as a means of making a class of AI attack known as prompt injections more stealthy. Malicious instructions embedded in emails or other untrusted content to be processed by an LLM aren’t written in ordinary text. Instead, they’re rendered by a special range of Unicode tags. For example, the tag point U+E0041 mirrors “A,” and U+E0061 mirrors “a.”
No longer just for obscuring prompt injections

The block of 128 tags mimics a portion of the American Standard Code for Information Interchange almost perfectly, with one major difference: the characters they encode are readable by computers but, by design, are almost completely invisible to humans. By expressing the malicious prompts in these tags, LLMs detect the instructions, but people reading the email never see them. There’s much more about ASCII smuggling here.

87b7e63bb77a5729: Malaysia’s next significant economic shift will not play out only in factories, data centres or capital markets. It will unfold around dining tables and in boardrooms, as wealth, businesses and responsibility pass from one generation to the next.

Most conversations about wealth still focus on building it. As Malaysia matures economically and demographically, a different question becomes just as important: how does wealth hold together once the person who built it can no longer lead?

The transition ahead is a substantial one. A generation of founders who built their businesses through the high-growth decades are approaching the point of handover; Malaysians are living longer, which often means leadership is held longer too.

Yet generational transitions are notoriously fragile and the reason is rarely commercial. Family enterprises do not usually falter at handover because they were unprofitable. They falter because nobody decided in advance who would make decisions, on what basis and with what accountability.

For family enterprises, that begins with three distinctions that are often collapsed into one. Ownership, management and beneficiary interest are not the same thing. A family member may own a share of a business without being the right person to run it and may be entitled to benefit from it without doing either.
Families that separate these questions before a transition tend to navigate it. Families that leave them entangled tend to litigate.

It also requires preparing the next generation rather than simply naming them. Stewardship is a capability, not an inheritance. Successors need exposure to the business, clarity about what is expected of them and an honest sense of what they are taking on - well before they are asked to take it on.

Structures support these decisions; they do not substitute for them. A conventional trust is an administrative arrangement designed for succession and wealth preservation, not an investment scheme. Used properly, it allows diverse family holdings to be administered within a single framework, so that a business is not fragmented across many hands at the worst possible moment.

As regional competition for capital intensifies, Malaysia’s ability to keep productive assets and family enterprises intact within stable, transparent structures bears directly on our economic resilience. Capital that fragments at every generational handover is capital lost to the wider economy.

The Securities Commission’s Practice Note and the forthcoming Trust Companies Bill are constructive developments. Clearer standards and clearer classification give families and institutions the confidence to plan over long horizons, and they strengthen Malaysia’s standing as a jurisdiction where wealth can be administered with integrity across generations.
A maturing framework is not a burden on this industry, it is what allows the industry to be taken seriously.

Wealth transition is not a test of investment performance. It is a test of stewardship. Founders who begin the transition early give their families and their enterprises a far better chance of carrying what they built into the next generation.
Muraly Daran is the director of a trust company and an FMT reader.
